subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in common with the
rest of the House I have a distinct feeling of friendship and admiration for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) but I am afraid it does not extend to his budget proposals. I am very glad, however, he has done one thing that I recommended a year ago-reduce the income tax on small incomes. It certainly will be gratifying to every working man and woman in this country, especially those with small incomes.
But on the question of tariff, I would have thought that the experience of the last four years would have been enough for even a Liberal administration, many of whose supporters I think are at heart ardent protectionists,-I would have thought it would have been enough for their feelings after contemplating the dire results of the small reductions they have made in the tariff in the last four years, to have left the tariff entirely to the advisory board which they have recently appointed. I would have thought they would have been satisfied, after losing from the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec approximately five hundred thousand of our young men and women to the United States during the last four years, cot to add more to that quota. The province of Ontario has been the chief sufferer from this exdflus. Presumably still more of our people will go to the United States now to secure the benefits of high protection which they find so advantageous to themselves. But when all is said and done it is really hard to understand why, having talked so much about the necessity of a tariff commission, the government did not trust this first article of tariff reform to that commission. However, after studying the situation carefully, and knowing the right hon. gentleman who is head of the newly formed Tariff Advisory Board, for whom both sides of the House have a high personal respect and admiration, I fancy the government did not think he would have enough strength of character to treat the tariff in this instance in a way that no supporter of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in his day and generation 14011-171,1
had ever thought of doing. Accordingly the government felt they had to give one great example of what should be done in this regard, and then the tariff board could proceed to mutilate the rest of the tariff as they might see fit. Should they follow this course and reduce the tariff to a maximum of 27 i per cent, which the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) says is sufficient for anyone, there would be practically no protection to our manufacturers and others under the existing conditions in this country.
Now, the peculiar reasoning of some people is that they seem to think we can maintain a low tariff alongside the United States, where they have followed consistently a policy of high protection. For instance, they give their automobile industry a protection ranging from 25 to 50 per cent according to the tariff imposed by other countries against American automobiles. But not only do the government of the United States protect their manufacturers and others with a high tariff, they have also a board sitting at Washington which apparently works night and day. Supposing we send into the United States any commodities w'hich the tariff board think might better be produced in their own country, the importer is invited to bring his samples to Washington or some other place where they may be examined, and if they do not happen to meet with the approval of the board's examiners, and those examiners think that the goods would be bought in the States, the importer is impeded and prevented from making deliveries and from bringing in any further supplies. This action is taken practically overnight, and in one case the tariff board increased the duty from 50 to 90 per cent.
Modern business is modern warfare. In other words, you cannot fight the United States or any other country along modern business lines unless you use their own weapons. Naturally, we would prefer to keep our people here. Obviously we cannot do-so unless they can earn as good wages as are offered them in the United States. Therefore -we should protect our manufacturers and working people against the importation of competing products from the United States and the countries of Europe. It is perfectly obvious that we cannot become a great and prosperous country unless we give fair and reasonable protection to the manufacturing interests of Ontario and Quebec and the other provinces, but particularly to those two great provinces, where there is an investment of nearly three billion dollars in industrial plants.
The Budget-Mr. Bristol

There are two classes in every community that I think are especially entitled to the fullest consideration. The first class are the farmers. We cannot possibly have a great and prosperous country unless our farmers are fairly treated, unless they have every reasonable opportunity of getting fair returns from the soil. We have the Progressive party in this House, of course, who for the most part are opposed to protection, but I do not know of any government in the provinces. Liberal or Conservative, that has not done all it possibly could for the farmers. It is well recognized to-day that our farmers produce the real wealth of the country to start with, and after them come our manufacturing industries. Nor do I know of any federal government in this country that has not tried to treat our farmers in a fair and reasonable way. Of necessity this must always be done if our country is to be successful. But we have two classes of farmers. There is the western farmer growing his No. 1 hard wheat. He is as fine a farmer as you will find anywhere in the world, and he grows the finest wheat that can be produced in any country. If he had free trade he would have practically no taxes to pay. On the other hand you have the farmer of Ontario, Quebec and the Mari-times who has to rely on other products of the farm, cheese, butter, eggs, and so on, which products have to meet competition the world over. There has been a failure on the part of the present government, and I regret to say of other governments also, to give the farmers of Ontario, Quebec and the Mari-times that fair and reasonable protection to which they are certainly entitled.
.But this is the worst phase of the situation. 'Ontario arid Quebec, for instance, are great producing provinces, the farmers there are prosperous, but those provinces are losing their population, their young men and women. Now, we cannot become a great nation unless we get our people to stay in the country and unless wTe get new population. Above all things, it seems to me the first duty of every 'government is to take care of the people of ''Ontario and Quebec; it is so to protect the industrial interests that the working people will have plenty of employment at as good wages as they could earn across the line, and the local farmers will have good customers. The next step should be to get back our boys and girls from the United States. No one can argue for a moment that the best settlers are not our own people, and we should make the country so prosperous and attractive that our people who have left will return; that those who are here will stay here and that

their number will be steadily added to by a constant flow of immigrants from the Old Country. But after four years of tariff reductions, resulting disastrously to the country, the government has decided apparently to put the finishing touch on their work, and thus drive a still greater number of our young people to the United States. Not only has the government seriously affected the automobile industry by this tariff reduction, but they have scared away capital. They are not doing anything, in other words, to retain our present population, yet new settlers are being brought into this country. We cannot go on with nine million people; with that population we cannot hope to keep paying our great debts and meeting our obligations and the expenses of government. We must have new population. We hear of schemes for bringing these people from England and other countries, but where are they to go? I suppose they will go to northern Ontario and chiefly to the west. I have not heard any particular outcry from those in the west that they want new settlement; in fact one of their leaders said that if they had no more farmers they could get on very well.
But I know that the spirit of fair play and the desire to do what is right exists in the west as well as anywhere else. When I put this position before my friends from the west I would like them to consider it well, because it means so much to Ontario and Quebec, as well as to the other provinces where manufacturing is carried on. People in any countiy have to pay taxes, of course; I think our western friends recognize that fact, and are willing to pay a fair share. It is better to keep the boys and girls in this country, employed in factories producing in Canada the goods which should be made here out of our own raw products, rather than allow goods to come in from the United States. That simply means that our money goes to the United States, and American labour makes a profit on what we buy. If you bring new settlers into Quebec certainly you will increase the home market, but the home market is not so important to the farmers of the west as is the world market. You have the best wheat in the world, and there is no trouble in disposing of it. But when you have the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec with their many farmers, that condition does not obtain.
If you shut down all these automobile factories, what will happen? First of all we will import a great many cars from the United States, with no proper tariff protection. One-half million of our young men went to the

The Budget-Mr. Bristol
United States in four years, and you will send another hundred thousand across the border if this course is pursued; you will frighten industry. If you want to have an agricultural country only then go ahead, because by tariff reductions that < 4 p.m. condition will be brought about.
We can, of course, manufacture lumber and paper, and we have great mineral wealth, but if you keep on with this policy there wi'll be very little else. This country has great natural resources; I do not think a low tariff could ruin Canada but it can do a great deal towards reducing our population and our prosperity. If we do not accord the farmers of Ontario and Quebec fair treatment we are going to injure them and destroy the farming interests in these two great provinces.
If we keep shutting down our factories with this sort of tinkering, and worse, the manufacturing interests of Canada will be greatly decreased and the farmers will lose their local markets. We have nearly three and a half billions of dollars invested in the manufacturing interests of Canada, and I suppose about seven billions of dollars in the farming interests, but one thing is sure: we have to treat each other fairly and reasonably, and I say to my hon. friends from the west that it is worth considering carefully whether it is not much wiser to let this automobile industry prosper as it has prospered in the past. If you want a reduction go at it cautiously, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier did, and then study the result. Such a large reduction as has been made is very detrimental to the public interest; the manufacturers are not able to tell exactly what is going to happen, and the people are uncertain also.
I have said that the farmers are entitled to every consideration, but I again say that the working men and women are entitled to even more consideration. Why? The working men and women of the country go home at the end of the week and take their wages with them; that is all they have, unless there is a small garden around the house or something of that kind. If they lose their jobs, which has already happened to some automobile workers, and which may happen to others in the next two or three weeks, although they may have saved a little money they are up against a very serious proposition. They will have to consider whether or not they should leave Canada, or what they can possibly do. The farmer, on the other hand, is in a different position. If he has a bad crop-which is a very serious thing, of course-usually he has enough produce around
his home, together with chickens, cows and farm animals of various kinds, to carry him through a winter even if he does no business at all. Of course, none of our farmers are in that position to-day; they are too skilful and too wise to put all their money into any one thing, even No. 1 northern wheat, and there is no doubt that the western farmer is progressing on broad lines. His is a wonderful country, and he will succeed. But the younger generation are entitled to every consideration from all of us, and I do not see why the working men and women of Canada should not be protected in this country, as is done in the United States. That country has a population of 120,000,000 people-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
permit a question?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I would rather not; I am
not trying to convince the hon. gentleman. We cannot hope to manufacture as cheaply as the United States, for obvious reasons. If you are making in a factory twelve times as much of the same article as another factory is making, obviously you can reduce your overhead to practically nothing, on large production, and your cost is very low. We have a tremendous opponent in manufacturing in our next door neighbours. They have vast wealth and are very fond of Canadians; they have certainly done everything possible to annex this country in a pleasant way. We are the only people in the world they are willing to admit without question, but when it comes to the articles manufactured in this country they put up a tariff wall and appoint an investigating committee, which shuts out everything which might compete with goods manufactured in the United States, and allows in only what they really need.
This is an easy country, Mr. Speaker, to make great and prosperous. We have a splendid population; I do not think there are any better people anywhere, any men, women, boys and girls more diligent or better behaved. We have the greatest natural resources of any country in the world1; it is said that at least S5 per cent of this country possesses mineral wealth. There is no doubt thajt we have power to an extraordinary degree, and the province of Quebec is particularly fortunate in that regard. What we must do in order to prosper is to treat each other fairly and squarely. The Maritime provinces have their troubles; they are entitled to every consideration. The western farmer has received, in my humble judgment, every consideration; he does not get protection, but his wheat is shipped down to the seaboard for
2G94
The Budget-Mr. Bristol

seven to nine cents a bushel less than American wheat is shipped over a similar distance. That is a big protection, when we consider our national railways and the amount of money we have expended in that connection. I would like to ask our western friends to consider the point of view of our manufacturing interests. It is far better to keep our young people in this country; to have our work done in Canada and to manufacture the raw products here, than to buy American products under any conditions. It may cost a little more, but the sacrifice will be a worthy one in the interest of Canada.
'So far as we in Ontario are concerned, we are hard-working people with every respect for the rest of the people of Canada, and we have every desire to see prosperity all over this great .Dominion. We have the friendliest feeling towards our next door neighbours in the province of Quebec. Some of us wonder occasionally why Quebec does not annex us, and1 then we would surely have a wonderful prosperity. I think that instead of trying to stay in office, whatever government it may be, we should look at the affairs of this country in the purely national way, not from a political point of view, and we should do the best according to our knowledge and ability to make our country great and prosperous.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, and the indulgence of the House, I should like to make a short contribution to the debate. First of all I must congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon the splendid programme which he has submitted. I think it is fair to say that the budget has been received with approval everywhere except by the automobile industries of Canada, and that it is on the whole pleasing to everybody. Of course it has not found favour with the industries to which I alluded and some hon. members opposite. The elimination of the receipt tax, the return to penny postage, the endeavour on the part of this government to route Canadian commerce through Canadian ports, the saving of $25,000,000 in taxes for the coming year, the conversion of an adverse trade balance of $29,000,000 into a favourable trade balance of $402,000,000 as a result of five years' administration, and the reduction of the national debt by some $22,000,000, are all matters for congratulation to the Canadian people. The budget has undoubtedly won compliments from the press of Canada, and in some instances the newspapers are loud in their praise of it. The one feature of the budget which has not met with an equally enthusiastic reception is the cut in the tariff, particularly on automobiles.
I Mr. Bristol. 1
Now, notwithstanding the fact that prior to the last general election the Conservative party preached generally throughout the country a campaign of blue ruin, and pointed to Canada as being in a deplorable condition and on the verge of bankruptcy, very little credit is being given by hon. members opposite to this government for the splendid condition existing in this country to-day. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) congratulated the Canadian people on the prosperous condition in which they found themselves, but declared that prosperity was entirely due to a beneficent Providence, a bountiful crop, and a virile Canadian people. At the same time he stated that the government of Ontario had put that province in a firm financial position by its able management. He gave credit to the government of Ontario for what it had done but declined to give any credit to the federal government for the prevailing prosperity. He asserted that Canada was only getting her due, she was only getting what was coming to her, that such advancement as the country had made should have come some two, three or four years earlier, and that there had been no improvement in the country during the last four years. The last statement is not entirely correct nor is it entirely fair. Let me point out that during the ten years the Conservatives held office in Canada, namely from 1911 to 1921, there was added to the national debt of this country the entire cost of the war, the entire cost of demobilization, and $170,000,000 besides. We all remember, looking back to the period immediately after the war, the depressed condition in which Canada found herself. At that time commerce and finance were stagnant, agriculture and industry were paralyzed. We well remember the credit of Canada had become very much impaired, and that the Canadian dollar was only worth some SO cents. We well remember that men and women were leaving Canada in hundreds and thousands, and even in greater numbers; that in the Dominion there was no money to be found, that this country had very little to sell, and that the price of such few products as she had to offer was not worth consideration. I had the novel experience, during that period of depreciation in the spring of 1918, of buying several hundred ewes at $25 apiece and selling them in the Winnipeg stockyards in the fall of 1921 for the paltry price of $2 each. That gives a pretty fair idea of the depression which prevailed in western Canada during that period. Mention was made in this House at the time of the condition in which Canada found herself, and when the government was appealed to for

The Budget-Mr. Howden
remedial measures it claimed that it could offer no remedy whatever. The Hon. Mr. Calder, speaking in the House on May 19, 1919, said:
I presume that the very large emigration from this country has been very largely due to the rapid expansion otf trade, a.nd commerce and industry of the United States in every direction, which has made opportunities for our young men to enter business there, and I dare say that condition wall continue.
He went on to say that on returning to his native town in Ontario he found that the young men whom he had known in his early days had all disappeared. Mr. McDonald, the former member for Timiskaming, made the following remark:
Some hon. members say that there are many idle men in Canada. We have in .t-hds country to-day the sorry spectacle of some 500,000 people who are idle and together with 'their dependents they number probably a million and a halt out of a population of perhaps ten millions. This is a sad spectacle indeed in this glorious land of ours which we profess to be so proud of. There are 500,000 men or thereabouts idle in Canada and we have bread lines in every centre of population in the country. Why the condition of affairs is staggering and the Dominion government is asked, if my information is correct, to contribute towards the sustenance of men in Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Montreal.
The Minister of Finance of the government of that day, speaking in the House said:
We in Canada have a great task before us. The world .is sadly out otf tune. Trust and confidence is sadly lacking. Class interests are advanced wiith selfish insistence. Unemployment is with us. Faith in our fellow men is weakened. Doubt of the future is voiced, and what is 'the trouble? The sun still shines, the rivers still sparkle and our lands are as fruitful as ever; our resources just as great.
This will give hon. members an idea of the condition of Canada at the time of which I speak. Now modesty is an ever-becoming virtue. I do not for a moment blame the government of that day for the condition in which Canada found itself. I do not suggest for a moment that the condition then could have been helped by the government of the time or by any government. The pendulum of fate ever swings, and at that particular time the odds were against Canada. I simply desire to point out that such was the condition which prevailed in this country subsequent to 1919 and up to the time the present government assumed office. Neither do I wish to give the Liberal government entire credit for the improvement which commenced to be apparent immediately after it entered upon its duties.
Now I will submit a few figures relevant to this matter, in order to show that a gradual improvement has taken place since the year 1921. When the present government came into office on March 31, 1922, the public debt
of this country stood at $2,422,000,000 in round numbers. On March 31, 1923, it was $2,453,000,000 and on March 31, 1924, it had been reduced to $2,417,000,000. On March 31, 1925, it was again $2,417,000,000, but in 1926, at the time of the present budget, we find the national debt reduced to $2,395,000,000, this being some $25,000,000 less than in 1922 and a saving of $22,000,000 from the last year, after providing an amount of $10,000,000 to the National Railways, and advancing $2,500,000 to the Home Bank creditors relief fund.
It has been claimed the government has been spending more money successively from year to year. The expenditures are as follows: in 1922, $464,000,000; in 1923, $434,000,000; a lessening of $30,000,000 from the year before. In 1924 it was $370,000,000.

speechtext:
Do those figures include
the railway expenditure, and if so do they include the railway guarantees?

speechtext:
I have taken these figures from the statistical department. They have been given to me under request and I am not able to answer my hon. friend's question accurately, but the figures I have given were supplied me by that department.
The expenditures in 1025 amounted to $350,000,000, and in 1926 they had been reduced to $342,000,000, but this does not include an advance of $10,000,000 to the National Railways, or $2,500,000 to the Home Bank creditors fund. I should like to point out also that in the year 1920-21 the public debt was increased by $92,000,000. In 1021-22 there was again an increase of $81,000,000, and in 1022-23 another increase of $30,000,000. For the year 1923-24 there was a decrease of $35,000,000. At this time a cut of $26,000,000 was made in the general taxation. Notwithstanding this fact there was still a surplus of $5,000,000, or a decrease of $31,000,000 in all, from the preceding year. We all know that in 1026 there has been another decrease of $22,000,000.
With regard to the charges of extravagance that were made by hon. gentlemen opposite, since the present government came into power the services of some 5,000 people have been dispensed with and this has caused a yearly saving of $5,000,000. I might point to the balance of trade also, and just briefly mention the fact that in 1921 we had an adverse balance of trade of $20,000,000, and that the condition has improved since, so that in the present year we have a favourable balance of trade of $402,605,000. Now in the face of these figures, no one can consistently ot

The Budget-Mr. Howden
honestly claim that there has been no improvement in Canada in the last four years. The -hon. member for South Wellington, in making the statement that this government had been an extravagant one, said, at page 2459:
I do say, however, that there are mfliians of dollars of suggested expenditures which might very well be deferred for some years to come without any inconvenience and with no ill effects on the Dominion.
Now, Sir, coming from Manitoba, this statement appears to have reference to the Hudson Bay railway. Without pausing to discuss that project at this time, I would like to say that the people of western Canada were looking for the completion of the Hudson Bay railway even before they were looking for the completion of the Canadian Pacific. Since the later seventies we have had the building of the Hudson Bay railway in mind. In the early eighties an appropriation was set aside fof the building of the road. There has been some $50,000,000 worth of land sold and some $30,000,000 collected, but up to the present time only some $20,000,000 has been spent and we of western Canada feel that the balance of these moneys should be used for the completion of that railway. With regard to the feasibility of the grain route via Hudson bay, which has been seriously questioned, I might say there have in the last hundred years come into Hudson bay some 675 ships with the loss of only two. It it not a very large number, but it is [DOT] about six ships a year, and the percentage of loss has been very small. Assuming the grain route to the Old Country via the Hudson bay never became useful, the Hudson Bay railway will find plenty of other commerce and industry to keep the route alive. I have been down the Nelson river some two hundred miles. There is a great deal of water-power all the way. I should imagine the country would be able to develop sufficient waterpower to pay for the upkeep of the line. Not only is this the fact, but the whole country is saturated with minerals; there is no doubt about that at all, and there is no way of getting these minerals out at the present time. There are large areas of pulpwood too in that country, and that is a matter worthy of consideration. The bay itself contains a wealth of fish life, producing the best salt water fish in the world. Even supposing which I do not admit by any means, that the grain route to the Old Country would be impracticable, there is no reason why the Hudson Bay route should not become a paying proposition.
The main criticism of the hon. member from South Wellington, is with regard to the proposed reductions in the tariff. The hon.

gentleman pointed to the fact that Ontario contains about one-third of the total population of the Dominion, and he stated that Ontario paid over one-half of the treasury receipts of the Dominion, that Ontario was the home of the automobile industry in Canada, that there were, in one way and another, engaged in -that industry, some 20,000 men, and that they with their families made up possibly 100,000 souls. He pointed out that the proposed reduction in the tariff on automobiles would1 probably greatly hamper the industry and possibly throw these men out of work. Now the statement of the hon. member is probably correct, so -far as Ontario is concerned, but I am by no means convinced that the proposed reduction in the tariff on automobiles is going to ruin the industry in Ontario and put these people out of employment. In support of that statement, I should like to read some of the remarks that were made by hon. members in the House to the effect that of the excess price paid by Canadians for cars, over the price paid on the same cars in the United States, less than half is paid for salaries and wages. The excess price of cars in Canada over cars in the United States is 40 per cent, more than one-third, and is it reasonable to suppose that the material going into the manufacture of these cars would cost the other two-thirds? I think not and for that reason I am disposed to believe that automobile dealers in this country reap fairly handsome profits from the manufacture and distribution of automobiles.
I should like also to put before the House some other statements that have been made by other hon. members. In ten different makes of cars -manufactured both in Canada and in the United States, the Canadian -price is from thirty-eight to forty-one per cent and in some cases nearly as much as fifty per cent higher than the United States price. Canadian made cars sell for a considerably lower price on the foreign market than they do in Canada. Cars of United States make assembled in Canada obtain a considerable drawback when exported and enjoy as well, under the British preference, a tariff of eleven per cent-on the British market, but these manufacturers take -advantage of all the tariff of thirty-five per cent will bear as regards the Canadian purchaser. Twenty million dollars in excess of United States prices on the same cars was paid by Canadian people to Canadian car-makers or assemblers in 1924. A Canadian firm which is well known to all, with an original capital of $125,000 -paid average yearly dividends of $642,000, that is to say over 500 per cent for a period of twenty

The Budget-Mr. Howden
years, and at the end of that period the total investment together with the total dividends amounted to $43,978,000 or a profit in twenty years of $43,853,000 on an investment of $125,000; that is to say an average yearly growth of over 1,800 per cent.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Where do those figures come
from?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Those figures were obtained by an hon. member of this House by direct interrogation of the managers of this particular automobile concern. Other firms are probably not quite so graciously favoured, but if an honest statement were made of their business as in the above case, it would doubless show that they too were making a very substantial return on their investment. Under the circumstances it does not seem to me that the automobile makers of this country are going to suffer very greatly by a reduction of fifteen per cent in the tariff on cheap cars.
The criticism, however, by hon. members opposite did not stop at the question of the tariff on automobiles; the tariff in general was mentioned. Since I have been interested in the political life of Canada I have heard continually of the necessity of raising the tariff on imported articles. That apparently is to be the cure-all for our ills in this country; but notwithstanding this fact, although the Conservatives were in power for ten years prior to the present government taking office, no effort was made by them to raise the tariff.
Comparisons are often made by our hon. friends opposite between Canada and the United States. The prosperity of the United States is pointed to by them and the fact that they have a high tariff is credited for being the reason for their prosperity. In Canada, although we are not quite so well off, we are rapidly regaining prosperity, and I believe the time is not very far distant when we shall have very little to complaiu of in that regard. Conditions in the two countries are very different. As was stated in this House last night, the United States entered the war some three years after the commencement of that great struggle and during those three years they were not only the storehouse but the merchant who supplied all the munitions of war and who lent the money. At the end of the war the United States of America found itself very rich as a result of that tremendous conflict. In Canada, on the other hand, we find a very different state of affairs. Canada was bled white of money, men and everything else; she was floundering under a stupendous load of debt for which no one can be blamed, and there was no sale for such products as she had for sale in those days for a simple reason. There had been over-production during the war and the world was practically overstocked with the necessaries of life, manufacturing and agricultural, so that there was no price forthcoming for what she had to sell.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: What is the per capita difference in debt between Canada and the United States?

speechtext: I cannot say.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I think hon. members will admit that conditions in the two countries were very different at the end of the Great war. There can be no question that the United States made a great deal of money as a result of the war and that Canada became practically bankrupt.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is not what hon. members opposite generally say.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, that is what I say. I am saying now that we are recovering and that is a very good thing. There is no question that we were in a very deplorable condition in this country at the end of the war. Apropos of this matter of the Canadian tariff I might point out that nearly fifty per cent of articles manufactured in Canada are exported and our manufactured exports have to compete in general with those of the United States, England and Germany on the world market. They receive no protection there and it is not probable that our manufacturers would export this material if they were going to lose money on it. How does this figure out? Our manufacturers take a chance on making what they can in the foreign market and they look to the people of Canada to protect them against any possibility of failure. That is to say, the tariff in this country is purely and simply a subsidy paid to Canadian manufacturers by the Canadian people through the medium of the Canadian parliament. Is this a very patriotic attitude? Does it seem to appeal to hon. members in this House or to the people throughout the country, that Canadian manufacturers should charge their own brothers greater prices for the commodities of life which they manufacture than they charge to the people to whom they sell abroad?
It is claimed by some hon. members that agriculture requires protection in the same manner as manufacturing industries. I am
The Budget-Mr. Howden

just wondering how you can protect the products of the western farmer. Is there any means by which you can put an export tax on our wheat or cattle and force the foreign buyers to pay us that extra money? Is it likely that if such an export tax were placed on raw materials we could get people to buy them from Canada? I do not think so. As a matter of fact we have to sell on the markets of the world whatever we produce and there we must take whatever price we can get, I do not see any good reason why the manufacturers should not do the same. The western agriculturist as an agriculturist has nothing whatever to gain from a tariff; it cannot help him in the least. We do not wish to take any selfish stand and we are willing, indeed we are anxious, to see Canada as a whole prosper. To this end we. are ready to make some sacrifice, but we do insist that this sacrifice be reasonable.
There is some possible question about the necessity for protection in respect of such things as fruit and early vegetables. As I have stated in this House before, early fruit and green leaf vegetables from abroad come into Canada before the products of this country are ready to be placed on the market, and the fact cannot be emphasized too strongly that these commodities are of extreme importance to the Canadian people. I want to read some remarks made by Doctor Hastings, the medical health officer of Toronto, at a recent medical convention. Doctor Hastings emphatically denounced any move which would add to the price of fresh vegetables in Canada in winter. He said:
I am absolutely opposed to it. My attitude is shown by the fact that I have been agitating for a complete removal of all duties from all citrus fruits. We should get our oranges, grapefruit and lemons duty free so that the price can be brought as near the poor man's ability to pay as possible. The leaf vegetables are of the greatest importance. Lettuce, spinach and cabbage would all come in duty free if I had my way in the matter.
At the same convention Miss Frances McNally director of the dietetics department of the Macdonald College, Guelph, had this to say:
W'hy, to shut the door upon or cut down the supply of leaf vegetables in Canada in winter would be little short of tragedy. Millions of dollars have been spent in educating the public to this value in dietary. To raise the price would be to throw away the results of years of educational work along this line.
We medical men all know that one of the greatest safeguards we have against the great white plague as also against a great many other constitutional derangements is suitable diet, and there is no suitable diet for constitutional diseases which does not include

green leaf vegetables and fresh fruit. I am inclined to believe, with Doctor Hastings of Toronto, that when fruit and early vegetables are available for Canada before the Canadian products are ready, even if these commodities come from the United States or from other places, they should be admitted free of duty. When we in Canada have our products ready for the market, then you can shut the other fellows out altogether so far as I am concerned; but I certainly think that until then the early fruit and vegetables should be allowed to come in free. This would redound to the benefit not only of the consumer but of the grower of fruit and green leaf vegetables in Canada as well.
I was interested to hear one hon. member from British Columbia state that he had seen wagonloads of apples taken to the dealers in towns throughout the fruit producing districts of that province, only to have them rejected, entailing the necessity of taking them back home, because there was no sale in view of cheaper American fruit being on the market. This is to me an astounding statement, especially when we know that to-day we have to pay five cents apiece for apples in any store in Ontario. When I was a little fellow in Winnipeg some forty years ago apples were at a premium; we thought when we were getting this fruit that we were getting a gold mine. But even at that time, as I remember, we could buy two or three apples for five cents as against one to-day. If therefore the fruit producers in this country are having to return home with wagonloads of apples because of the duty the condition of affairs is indeed strange.
I do not think it is necessary to refer to butter and eggs. A good deal has been said about butter in connection with the Australian treaty, which, it is said, is injurious to the trade in Canada. I am safe in saying, I believe, that there is not much butter manufactured in Canada in winter, the vast bulk of our product being made wdien the cows are in full milk in summer. The milk and cream offered for sale in Canada in the winter months goes directly to the dining tables of the land as such. The fact is that our butter is being made in summer when cream is plentiful and being stored by the creameries and the cold storage plants, if anyone suffers through the admission of Australian butter it cannot be the primary producer; it must be the operators of the cold storage plants and possibly the creameries. Pretty much the same thing holds in regard to eggs, for we know that the bulk of our eggs is produced in Canada between the first of March and the

The Budget-Mr. Howden
end of June. As a general rule the hens begin to moult in July, and they do not then lay for some six weeks or two months. There are therefore few eggs laid in the fall, and those few never leave the farm. The Canadian market is supplied with the production that takes place between the first of .March and the last of June, and the cold storage houses also put away large quantities of this commodity during this period. I heard the statement made in this House recently that only one egg in ten used in Canada was of domestic production. This impelled me to secure certain statistics from the bureau, and after figuring the matter up I find that very much the opposite is the case: sixty Canadian eggs are used in this country for every one that is imported. The surplus Canadian eggs are held by the cold storage plants until the months of September, October and November, when they are put upon the market, those months being the season of the year in which eggs are scarce. We have very few eggs produced in Canada during fall and winter months, except those that come from the poultry farms and which are sold as newlaid eggs at prices beyond the reach of ordinary incomes. We have to depend upon the eggs that come in from the southern states. These are practically fresh eggs, and to shut them out by a high tariff would be to do an injury to the rank and file of the Canadian people.
In common with a great many others, I believe that we Canadians should bend our energies to. the development of our basic industries, and encourage the manufacture only of such materials as are obviously Canadian in origin. What are our basic industries? There are many, but obviously agriculture is the leading one, and the chief feature of agriculture is the production of wheat and grain. There can be no question about it that agriculture is our chiefest basic industry, although we have others such as lumbering, mining and fishing. But since the wealth of any land must come from the soil it is clear that agriculture is and must be the most important basic activity of any people. There can be no question that agriculture is the most important basic industry of this country. Can wre develop any industries in connection with agriculture? Well, we have some. Of course, we can mill our grain and make flour. There is a contention in the west that the flour ought to be milled where the wheat is grown. There are difficulties, however, in the way of this which make it almost impossible. In the first place it is stated there is no market for our flour abroad. This is hardly correct, for we sell quite a large amount of our best
Canadian flour on foreign markets. But it is pointed out with a great deal of truth that England is a workshop, that they do not want our flour but want our grain, which they themselves will make into flour and distribute. That is only the half of the story. They not only want our wheat to mill, but they want it to mix with the wheat from the other great wheat-growing countries of the world, and thereby make a better grade of flour. So it looks as if we would have to be content with manufacturing flour for our own consumption. It is also pointed out that it is much cheaper to export whole wheat than flour and its by-products.
With respect to our mining industry, I heard it stated recently that Canada contains the only commercial nickel in the world, that Canada and South Africa have the only commercial deposits of asbestos in the world, and that in Canada are to be found deposits of lead and zinc superior to those in any other country. Unfortunately I am not sufficiently familiar with this industry to speak freely, but it seems to me reasonable enough to take the position that if the world is dependent on Canada for nickel, asbestos, lead and zinc it ought to come to Canada and get those products in their highest stage of manufacture. I do believe that a scheme ought to be worked out whereby our mines should be protected and the whole benefit of our mineral deposits accrue to the Canadian people.
As to our fishing industry, our export trade is considerable. We have a vast supply of fish in our rivers, in the inland lakes and in our seaboard waters, and this is an important form of our natural wealth.
With regard to our timber, I think that also ought to be very generally processed in this country before it is allowed to be exported.
There are other manufacturing industries which do not rely on any of our natural products. For instance, I understand that all the materials for the silk manufactured in this country have to be imported from Europe. I do not very well see how an industry of this kind can be expected to compete with the long-established and highly specialized silk industry of the Old Country.
The same remarks apply to the manufacture of paint. Not very long ago I visited a paint works in the city of Winnipeg and listened to a very instructive lecture by the superintendent in regard to the manufacture of paint, in the course of which he pointed out that they brought their materials from all over the world. Just how they can hope to compete with districts where the raw materials are very much more easily secured is not obvious to me.
The Budget-Mr. Howden

I might point out to the House we have not very many industries in the prairie provinces. I think it would be rather a good scheme for our protectionist friends to try to infiltrate those provinces with a few industries. I have always wondered why there are so few industries established throughout the west. I have heard it suggested the probable reason is that we cannot get them financed. I think every hon. member will agree that the money-power of this Dominion is pretty well centered in eastern Canada around Toronto and Montreal. When a man in the west desires to go into an industry his bank manager says, "Very well, but I think you had better run down east and see the president of the bank." When the man gets there the president says, "What is the idea of manufacturing up in that wilderness? WThy not bring your industry down here? Of course, we will finance you all right, but it will be very much easier to finance you here." The consequence is that pretty nearly all our industries are centered in eastern Canada. I am not at all sanguine of their success, but I would suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that if they want to change the minds of western Canadians on tariff matters they had better establish a few industries out there; then they may be able to make some of our people protectionists.
With regard to the amendment that has been offered by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), it gives no definite intimation as to the attitude of our friends opposite in relation to what they would like the government to do in the matter. A few days ago the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) stated that he was not in favour of taking the tariff out of the hands of parliament, and he read extracts in support of his view. He said that by all means the proper authority to deal with tariff questions was the parliament of the land. We on this side are wondering why hon. members opposite did not intimate what line they thought should be taken with regard to the budget alterations, or if any alterations at all should be allowed to take place. I am inclined to wonder if a good many hon. members on the other side are not actually in favour of a reduction in the tariff on automobiles, and if it is not a little bit difficult for them to come to a conclusion amongst themselves as to just what they actually want. If they had definitely intimated just what they would like done, vre would be very much further ahead. As it is, they merely point out that they wish the whole tariff referred to the Tariff Advisory Board. This would hold up the budget for an indefinite period.

That does not change the situation at all. We are still quite at a loss to go ahead and meet the wishes of hon. gentlemen opposite.
I will only delay the House a few moments, to mention the Canadian National Railways. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) gave the entire credit for the Canadian National Railways to the right hon. leader of the opposition, which reminded me of a story my mother used to tell some years ago about an old Irishman who was never a great success in life himself but whose boys grew up and prospered. The old man used to take the credit for the successful career of the boys, and would interrogate the members of his family in this way, "Aren't yez proud of yer owld father, that can have such foine sons?" I was thinking that the right hon. leader of the opposition was being placed in precisely the same position.
With regard to the Canadian National Railways I would say, "Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's." Far be it from me to detract from any credit due to the right hon. leader of the opposition, for whom personally I have a very high regard. In the matter of the Canadian National Railways, not being very familiar with the facts, I am willing to admit that the scheme was perhaps conceived by hon. members opposite, led by the right hon. leader of the opposition, and a great deal of the programme put in action by them. It must be admitted, however, that at the time this government took office the Canadian National Railways was a white elephant. It was like the ugly duckling; no one wanted to father it at the time. Now that the system has been put on a paying basis through the efforts of this government in the appointment of Sir Henry Thornton and in other ways, we believe that a great deal of credit for this very excellent public utility should be given to this government.
In this connection I might quote some figures with which a good many hon. members are familiar, but I will just pause long enough to say that in the year 1921 the operation of the railway alone showed a deficit of $11,000,-

The Budget-Mr. Clark
000. This deficit has disappeared and the position has been gradually improved, so that this year we have a surplus of $32,000,000 in the operation of that road.
I believe I have exhausted my material. I am not a very rank politician, and I believe that after all there is not such a tremendous difference between members of this House. I believe we are all perfectly honest, and that we are expressing our views, our sentiments, our beliefs and our convictions as we feel them. I think we are all working for the betterment of Canada and that Canada in no very distant future will be perhaps the favoured land of the world. We are still in the morning of our day; with our cousins to the south it is high noon, and in the 5 p.m. Old Country the day is perhaps well spent. But, Sir, I have enough faith in this country and in the Canadian people to believe that in the very near future we will build a great nation here; we will be the finest dominion on the face of the earth, and I trust that I shall not be damned for my temerity in so thinking.

I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Howden) will not expect me to review his address in detail. I may say that I enjoyed his remarks very much, but I fear we do not agree in many matters of policy affecting this Dominion. There are one or two observations I would like to make in connection with his remarks. I would draw his attention to the fact that if there was a bread line of 500,000 people in Canada when this government came into office, those people have not since found employment through any efforts of this government; they are now in the United States, enjoying employment there.
Mr. hon. friend quoted the expenditures of this government since it assumed office, in an effort to show that there had been some economy effected. I do not dispute the figures which my hon. friend quoted; they included the railway expenditures, but my hon. friend was not here when this government covered up the actual railway expenditures by guaranteed bond issues, which are not shown in the expenditures referred to. The only way my hon. friend can arrive at any idea of the expenditures of this government is by referring to the public accounts. I have the public accounts for 1925 under my hand, and I would draw attention to the fact that in only one year since this government assumed office was there any material reduction in the ordinary and capital expenditures, exclusive of railway expenditure. That was in
the year 1923, when there was a reduction c.' $15,000,COO, largely due to a reduction in war expenditures. There was a reduction in 1924 of $6,000,000 only; a reduction in 1925 of $4,000,000 only, and I draw attention to the fact that, according to the statement made by the Minister of Finance in this House on April 15, the 1926 expenditures show a very large increase over those of 1925. The expenditures shown for 1926 are $342,890,000, whereas the expenditures for the year previous were $339,902,775.94, a very substantial increase.
I would further call attention to the fact that while the estimates for 1926-27, as the minister pointed out, only show a drop of about $4,000,000, the minister admitted that these estimates do not include the supplementary estimates, which will ordinarily run from $7,000,000 to $10,000,000. These estimates do not include about $12,000,000 for old age pensions; they do not include the sum required to take care of the revaluation of soldier lands, nor do they include, unless I am mistaken, anything for the Empire land settlement scheme. Neither do they make provision for rural credits, which may require many more millions of dollars. Thus a very conservative estimate of the expenditures for the forthcoming year would be $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 in excess of the expenditures of the previous year.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want this interchange to develop into a debate between myself and the last speaker because there are several very vital matters I would like to touch upon.
I think the House will agree with me when 1 say that the two outstanding features of this budget are the so-called income tax reduction, and the reduction in the duties on automobiles. I propose to refer briefly to the income tax reduction. Undoubtedly there is a reduction on small incomes earned, by salaried people who do not receive dividends from corporations. That is obvious. I was very much interested the other day when the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) spoke on this subject and joined in the general jubilation over the fact that the income tax had been drastically cut on incomes which equal the indemnity of a member of parliament. That was very interesting, particularly after the hon. member's speech in the early part of the session on the Address when he said emphatically that the government should go slow in the matter of any income tax reduction. Now, according to the Minister of Finance these reductions are very substantial. But no word of protest came from my hon. friend that the tax has been removed from that portion of the people who can pay, nor did I hear him raise his voice for the vast body of the common people, for whom he is so fond of talking, and protest against the fact that the sales tax in Canada raised by this government and resulting in an average annual increase since it assumed office of twenty-two and a half million dollars in taxation, is continued. That tax is paid by the common people, and that is the tax which will continue to be extracted from their pockets. I wonder what the common people

of this country will say when they hear of that? I wonder what they will say when it really sinks into their minds what these reductions mean to them? Are the common people those who receive salaries of 13,000 and upward, or are they the people who are in receipt of salaries under that amount? If I am not mistaken the great bulk of the Canadian people receive salaries under $3,000, yet no relief is given to them. They are told that this extra twenty-two and a half million dollars of taxation imposed by this government will continue to be extracted hereafter. There you have the budget for the common people whose interests hon. gentlemen to my left so often profess to defend in this House. I wonder if the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) will approve of this cut in taxation in the interest of those who can pay, and will stand up and vote for the continuance of taxation on the common people, for the extraction of increased taxation to the amount of twenty-two and a half million dollars annually, imposed by this government and continued under this budget?
As to the question of the income tax reductions, may I say this? It is a matter of great surprise to me that the imposition of this income tax has never been legally contested by the corporations of Canada, because I know that although the reduction in income tax under the budget is held as a great thing for the people of the Dominion, yet out of collections amounting to $56,000,000 nearly $32,000,000 is paid by the corporations and an additional $14,000,000 is paid by the manufacturers, making $46,000,000 in all paid by the manufacturers and the corporations of Canada combined. To what extent are these two classes relieved by this budget? The income tax paid by the corporations is reduced, I think from 10^ per cent to nine per cent. That will not account for a reduction in excess of $3,000,000 unless, due to the acts of this government a number of these corporations go out of business this year, and I am inclined to expect that. But if business continues as it has continued during the past year these corporations may pay $3,000,000 less than they paid last year. On the other hand the manufacturers who are paying $14,000,000 will now pay in excess of that amount because they are taxed this year on their dividends, whereas last year their dividends were relieved from the normal tax although they paid the surtax. This year the particular class that pays the $14,000,000 will pay, I venture to say, in excess of what they paid last year. And when the Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Clark
Finance predict-s that this is a reduction in the income tax I question it very much. There is a reduction, as I said before, of income tax in the case of such people as earn an amount equal to the indemnity of a member of parliament, but not in the case of the class that actually pays the great portion of the income tax in Canada.
I repeat, the two classes that pay are the corporations and the manufacturers. All but about $10,000,000 of the total income tax is paid by these two classes. I mentioned that I was surprised that the imposition of this tax had never been tested by any corporation. Note the ingenious manner in which the Minister of Finance referred to this feature in his speech the other day. He stated that the special war revenue taxes received during the fiscal year 1925-26 amounted to $154,580,000, and added:
The total expenditures directly attributable to the war

and I desire to especially direct this to the attention of the House

will amourot to some $163,997,000, or $9,417,000 more than the receipts from our special war revenues.
Now the minister knows better than I do that that statement is not in accord with the facts and not in accord with the public accounts of Canada. Some time ago I received a statement, in answer to a question, which showed an increase of $121,896,099 in the interest on the public debt since 1914, and the Minister of Finance attributes that whole increase to expenditures due to the war. Now that amount is nearly double the amount of interest on the public debt due to the war, as I see it. The Minister of Finance asks this House and the country to believe that prac-ticallj' the total national debt to-day is directly attributable to the war and that the debt has not been increased by cash advances of nearly $600,000,000 to the railways, for instance. The public accounts of Canada for 1925 show that the total cost not only of the war but of demobilization was $1,694,365,809.60. If that whole amount is charged up to or added to the national debt, it does not account for more than sixty per cent of the total interest which the Minister of Finance attributes to the increase on the debt due to the war. I wonder if the minister makes that statement in order that he may be on safe ground, in case the 'legality of the direct income tax for purposes other than the war is tested? Because I say emphatically that the special war taxes now collected by this country exceed by many millions the sum required to take care of war expenditure, and in so far as income tax is applied to purposes other than special war purposes it is ultra vires of the parliament of Canada, parliament having no power to impose direct taxation for anything other than war purposes.
I should like to give a concrete illustration of the effect of the present income tax proposals on a business that makes net profits of $55,000. That might be considered a comparatively small corporation. At nine per cent that corporation will pay a tax of practically $5,000, leaving for distribution about $50,000. Assuming there were ten equal shareholders in that company, each would receive in dividends $5,000. A year ago these shareholders would not have paid income tax on those dividends. I am not sure whether I am absolutely correct in that; I know I am correct up to $4,000. In any case none of it was subject to the normal tax of four per cent, and I do not think the surtax would come into operation on an income of $5,000. This year, on the other hand, those ten men, each one of whom would have paid $495 by way of income tax into the revenues of this country through the Corporation tax, will pay an additional sum greater than the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) who is so jubilant because his income tax is being reduced, will pay on his $4,000 indemnity. That will be accentuated in the case where a shareholder of a corporation receives very large dividends. The Minister of Finance stated it was his desire that such moneys might find their way back into industry, but as a matter of fact there will be less available to go back into the industry this year than there was last year.
I turn now, Mr. Speaker, to the reduction of the tariff on automobiles. The only reason given therefor by the Minister of Finance or by his government, was that there was a pronounced sentiment in Canada that the automobile industry was receiving too much protection. Well, since when have governments brought down sentimental legislation? Why was some reference not made to the pre-election pledges of the Prime Minister in this connection? Why was no reference made to the solemn pledges that appeared in the Speech from the Throne? I think it might be well to refer to two or three utterances of the Prime Minister during the campaign, as to how he felt when he appealed to the voters of Canada for their support. I refer to a speech made at Kingston, reported in the London Advertiser of October 20, in which the Prime Minister is quoted as saying:
"We realize that our industries here have to have safeguarding with respect to competition from other parts of the world, competition from the country to the south, competition from conditions as they are :n Europe, and we think that is all the more reason why
The Budget-Mr. Clark

in these days of depreciated currencies and the like we should have the benefit of expert advice and information on all these great questions of the tariff.
This city of Kingston need have no fear from Liberal administration as to the well-being of its industries. The industries would be taken care of. The government had no desire to injure established industries, quite the contrary."
Speaking at Fort William on October 12th, the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
''We don't want to work injury to any industry." he urged, ''we want to help, as far as possible, all industries. We hope to make such readjustments of the tariff as will develop the industrial life of our country from one end of the country to the other."
He referred to a Fort William starch factory. He had, he said, been asked if It would not be possible to give home industries more protection and get the industry started again.
''How in such a case," asked the Prime Minister, ''would the tariff board proceed? We would," Mr. King continued, ''expect the member of the division to go before the board and present the case of that industry. We would expect a deputation of persons interested; then we would expect the tariff board to make a careful study of the whole subject and say whether some readjustment of the tariff could not be made here and there.
If we were advised that a readjustment could be made of the tariff schedule that would serve to put. the great industry on its feet again without undue injury to consumers the government would certainly be inclined to accept in a sympathetic way any suggestion of that sort. In revising the tariff there would be no intention of protecting special interest."
If inquiries of the board, however, might show that in some cases the tariff would have to be lowered, in some cases there might have to be readjustments here and there upwards. The aim would be to have a tariff suited to the needs of the country and to needs of the people. I
I have many other utterances of the Prime Minister along similar lines, but these suffice to show that he gave his word to industry in this country that no industry would be affected by any adjustment of the tariff without a proper investigation by the tariff board. I would like to ask the Prime Minister why he has broken his word to the Canadian people? I would like to ask the government why they have broken their solemn pledges, given in the Speech from the Throne, that all industries would be investigated by the tariff board before any revision upwards or downwards took place. Apparently they are dumb. Attempts have been made to bolster up the position of the government by some of my friends to the left and some of my friends from Saskatchewan. The government could find no reason except that of sentiment. Their friends have been floundering around trying to find some reasons, all of which are just as ridiculous as the reason advanced by the government that they were doing this for sentimental reasons.
The hon. member for Brandon, in his efforts for the benefit of the common people, wants

to get cheaper cars for them. I do not think the common people in this country are as much interested in getting cheap cars as they are in being relieved of the burden of taxation imposed by this government and also in finding employment and in retaining the employment which they now have.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) said: "The profits in this industry are too great." Is that not one reason why the tariff board was established, so that these questions might be referred to them for investigation in order that they might ascertain the profits and determine w'hether or not they were too great?
He made another suggestion, namely, that it would be more patriotic on the part of the Canadian people to buy United States' cars and to pay the duty than to buy Canadian cars made by our own Canadian workmen. He supports that argument by certain figures. He states that if in 1924 we had imported all our cars, the Canadian government would have received $20,000,000 by way of customs revenue, whereas, he says, as a matter of fact they received only in the neighbourhood of $1,581,882. I will do my hon. friend this justice; I do not dispute these figures because I have not investigated them. But I have the corresponding figures for 1926 from the Customs department, and they show that if all cars sold in Canada last year had been imported the customs duty would have been about $17,000,000. They show that the net customs duties paid by automobile manufacturers, after drawbacks are deducted, are about $4,500,000. The automobile manufacturers themselves say that they paid net duties, after allowing for all drawbacks, amounting to $7,418,513. I take their statement without hesitation because I know they import many articles which are not classified as automobile parts. In addition to that about two hundred "parts" men have stated that they pay in duties $1,168,411, making a sum of $8,586,925 net payment to the Canadian customs for the year 1926. There is a considerable difference between $17,000,000 and $8,586,925, but the House should bear in mind that this industry paid also $2,000,000 in income taxes. A considerable sum paid' by "parts" manufacturers is not reported and there is a certain amount of income tax paid by 22,000 men employed in this industry.

speechtext: I do not think I am bound to answer my hon. friend. I have a statement from the Department of Finance showing, as I stated before, that corporations in Canada paid $32,000,000 of the $56,000,000 in income tax and that manufacturers paid an additional $14,000,000, making a total of about $46,000,000 paid by corporations and manufacturers. It is pretty safe to assume that the automobile industry paid $2,000,000. I took those figures from public statements made by the automobile industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is all right.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I rely on them and I do not think my hon. friend will dispute them. I hope the Minister of Finance will not dispute the fact that these 22,000 employees in the automobile industry and subsidiary industries pay some income tax and that they also contribute a part of the enormous sales tax that is being collected in this country. The burden of the sales tax bears on those employees and they are subscribing very largely to it. I do not think the Minister of Finance will dispute the fact that their hundred thousand dependents pay a considerable amount into the Customs department of the $120,000,000 odd collected by that department, nor will he dispute the fact that they pay some stamp taxes. Let me say just here that this stamp tax has grown since this government came into office from, approximately $2,000,000 to about $9,000,000,

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Prosperity.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
No, increased taxation.
When this government-came into office a two cent stamp had to be put on a cheque. Now it is more likely to be a dollar. Last year in my own very small office in Vancouver, I cannot give the exact figure, but I know the stamp taxes were much in excess of $250, so that my hon. friend can see how heavily this tax bears on the people of Canada. The Minister of Finance may well take off some of the income tax when he increases the stamp tax to $9,000,000, a tax that does not bear fairly on the Canadian people. It is the people who are paying out money or borrowing money for their needs who are taxed for that privilege.
Now, referring again to other contributions made to the revenue of the country by these individuals, I venture to say that their payments to the provincial and municipal governments are almost as great as to the federal revenue, and possibly greater. So that when hon. gentlemen have the hardihood to suggest that it is more patriotic to buy American cars than to maintain the Canadian industry by 11011-172
keeping on the duties, I say that any simpleton can sit down and figure out for himself just what this industry means to the treasury of the Dominion. The automobile industry and its employees pay probably 100 per cent more in taxes than would be paid in duties by the Canadian people if they imported all their cars from the United States.
I think I am well within the mark when I say that they pay in taxes to the Dominion and to the provincial and municipal governments a sum not less than $30,000,000.
The hon. member who last spoke (Mr. How-den) implied that the wages paid to the employees in this industry were not great in comparison to the value of the finished product. I will do him the justice to admit that he was fair: he did say that a substantial sum was paid in wages, but he qualified the statement. I am sorry he is not here, because I would point out to him that in this industry considerably over sixty per cent of the value of the finished product consists of materials. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), in a speech he delivered in this House a few weeks ago made the statement that the total wages paid in the automobile industry were insignificant in comparison with the total value of its output. Once more let me say, the manufacturers of automobiles in Canada assert that they pay in salaries and wages the sum of $17,595,282, while the subsidiary industries which manufacture automobile parts declare that their payroll amounts to $14,036,668. My good friend from Macleod referred particularly to the Ford industry, stating that the wages paid amounted to about $7,000,000 as against a total production valued at something like $8S,000,000.	He had the Ford statements
before him, and I am sure they cannot be controverted, for the Ford people would not risk giving false returns. Well, those returns show that their expenditures in materials in Canada during the last year amounted to approximately $20,000,000. These materials consisted of such things for example, as automobile wheels. Now surely it requires labour to produce automobile wheels, so that a great deal of that $20,000,000 would represent wages paid to labour.
And would it be suggested by anyone that of the $7,775,000 paid in freights by the automobile manufacturers and subsidiary corporations last year a considerable proportion does not represent employment to the Canadian people? What will be the effect upon Canadian railways if we import automobiles from the United States? I know what the effect will be in British Columbia: automobiles will be assembled in Seattle and will be shipped

The Budget-Mr. Clark

over the Great Northern railway into Vancouver instead of over the Canadian National railway from Toronto or Walkervi'lle. They will come over American roads from New York and thence by way of the Great Northern into Vancouver, and into Winnipeg and other prairie points. Furthermore, when a commodity is manufactured in Canada it means that the railways move at least four carloads of freight to every one that is moved if the article is imported in the finished state, because there is the hauling of raw materials to the factory to be considered. I have no doubt every manufacturer will agree with me that at least four carloads of freight will move in the case of the article manufactured at home as against one when the finished product is imported.

I think you will agree with
me, Mr. Speaker, that I have been franker with my hon. friend than he has been with me. I state unhesitatingly that I would put the duty back to 35 per cent and turn the tariff board loose on the industry. I am in accord with the policy announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his election pledges; I am in accord with the policy announced by the government in the solemn pledge given in the Speech from the Throne, that no industry would suffer without 
investigation. This government has broken its pledges; the Prime Minister has not kept his word to the people of Canada, and all that one needs to do to prove this is to read the statements I have quoted this afternoon.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
