I have not spoken to my leader, nor have I discussed this particular question with any member of the party on this side, but I am sure that the feeling of hon. gentlemen over here would be that the duty should be put back to 35 per cent, and the industry investigated by the tariff board.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I should like to see the Manitoba Tories vote for it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
They will vote all right;
the Minister of Agriculture need not worry.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am not worrying at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I come from a constituency in which neither automobiles nor automobile parts are manufactured, and there is jusi as much likelihood of the reduction being popular there as it will be on the prairies. But I am man enough to stand up and declare that I want to see justice done to the people of Canada, no matter where they may be located, whether in Ontario, in Saskatchewan or anywhere else. And I say that justice has not been done in this case. A grave injustice has been done, and the Minister of Agriculture is a party to it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Has the
hon. member seen the statement of Mr. Ford in this morning's papers?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes. Would not Mr. Ford just love to see free trade in this country? Would it not have been a great thing for Mr. Ford if no tariff had ever been put on against the importation of American automobiles? Do you think Mr. Ford wanted to come to Canada to manufacture cars? Did any other American firm want to come here to manufacture for the Canadian market? Would they not have been delighted to supply the Canadian market from their United States factories? And would not Mr. Ford have made infinitely more money out of Canadians if there had been no tariff? Let me tell my hon. friend what happened. The Ford Company of Detroit was started with a

The Budget-Mr. Clark
capital of $28,000. To-day it has net profits in excess of $100,000,000 a year-profits largely in excess per car of the profits made by the Canadian Company. Now then, the Canadian Company commenced with a capital of $125,000.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: How much cash?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Last year the profits of
that company were quoted by an hon. member at about $6,100,000. The stock valuation of the Ford Company in Detroit has grown to $6,000 per share; that of the Ford Company of Canada to $425 per share. But since the government announced its policy the stock has dropped 160 points.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hit it again.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I realize that that is the
policy of my hon. friend from Saskatchewan. I am not here to defend the Ford Company or any other manufacturer. What affects me is this: there are very few automobile manufacturers that have not got their main plants in the United States, and they would just as soon go back there to-morrow and supply the Canadian market. But I do believe in some sense of justice, in some sense of fairness on the part of members from Saskatchewan towards those 22,000 workers and their 100,000 dependents who are located in one small part of Ontario-a province which, by the way, contributes 50 per cent of the total revenues of this country. I appeal for fairness to a province that is able to do that. It is not my province, but I do feel, no matter what province it may be, our object should be to keep good Canadian people here.
It might be well at this point for me to mention that the Ford Company of Canada, for instance, since 1913, has made price reductions of 41 per cent, while during that time all other commodities have increased in price, so that it takes to-day $155 to purchase what $100 would have purchased in 1913. That reduction, I believe, is due largely to two things:	keen competition among the
manufacturers of cheap cars, and the economies effected by the Ford Company at Ford, Ontario, through mass production.
Why does it cost more to manufacture automobiles in Canada? I have only to refer the government to its own returns for 1925, which show a drawback of customs duty on automobile parts amounting to $4,426,S01.66, and an export value of automobiles totalling $26,030,339. The drawback was one-sixth of the total value, or slightly over 16 per cent. That increased cost of manufacturing a car in Canada is due to the imported parts that 14011-1721
enter into its manufacture. I think that is of sufficient importance to repeat in another form. It is said on all sides, "Why cannot these Canadian manufacturers turn out cars as cheaply as they do in the United States"? Well, it is a comparatively new industry to this country; many of the component parts are not yet manufactured here, and the domestic market for automobiles has not yet warranted the erection of Canadian factories to manufacture those parts. The manufac- . ture of parts is already a considerable industry in this country, but there are still many parts, particularly engines, that cannot be manufactured here. It will probably take some time before we can develop the automobile industry so that the whole manufacture is done in Canada. In the meantime the cost of production throughout the whole industry is increased by 16 per cent on cars for distribution in Canada by reason of the customs duties paid on imported parts. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance is smiling at my remarks or not, but let me tell him I am not now quoting figures supplied by the automobile manufacturers, I am quoting figures furnished by the Customs department. That one feature alone increases the cost of manufacture in this country tremendously.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I do not think the average Canadian manufacturer to-day is in a position to produce 50 per cent of the car.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: That is the milk in the cocoa-nut-that is what all the row is about.

speechtext:
I think the minister will agree that our manufacturers have increased their percentage of manufacture tremendously in the last few years. Then again, the manufacturer will be put to so much trouble in applying for rebates on his parts that it will require an extra staff and the cost will be almost prohibitive. At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was dealing with the statement of the Minister of Finance that there will be a 25 per cent rebate of duties
The Budget-Mr. Clark

paid on parts imported for the further manufacture of motor cars, and I think I had given three reasons why that would not be of any material advantage to the industry. In order to take advantage of that rebate it will be necessary to manufacture fifty per cent of the car in Canada. Now that I admit is a very laudable ambition, it is one to which we all aspire. But the very effect of a reduction in the duties on parts will be to cause even less of the ear to be manufactured in Canada than at present, because the manufacturers will be forced to buy the parts where they can buy them the cheapest; they will naturally import more parts from the United States where mass production is carried on and where the parts are cheaper. One instance of the effect of mass production is given by the Ford industry, the only automobile industry in Canada which has reached a high percentage of production in Canada. I understand that the figure is from 80 to 90 per cent. However, that industry, as we all know, is not one which is most affected by the cut in the tariff; it is the least affected although it is the industry which this government aimed at when it reduced the tariff. I think that other manufacturers of motor cars in Canada have hardly reached the fifty per cent basis. I doubt if many of them have got beyond forty per cent, although the percentage has undoubtedly increased in the last few years; it is on the increase to-day, and if the industry were given a fair chance that increase would in the very near future reach a figure well in excess of the fifty per cent.
May I point out to the Minister of Finance that the wages and the purchases of the automobile industry indicate the enormous value to Canada of that industry? First of all, the wages paid by the manufacturers themselves and their subsidiaries amount to $3l'.500,000. Then as to the very large purchases, two instances might be given. Ford purchases in Canada, $32,431,000 worth of goods, though he only sells to Canadians to the extent of $25,914,000, leaving for circulation in Canada the enormous sum of $6,716,840. Another instance might be given, the General Motors. They make purchases in Canada of Canadian materials amounting to $35,733,390, whereas they only sell to the Canadian people goods to the value of $34,044,048, leaving a balance for circulation in Canada of $1,689,342, And may I state, so far as Ford is concerned at any rate, that because he produces from 80 to 90 per cent in Canada, very little of the money received by that company gees out of this country. For instance last year I think the company declared in dividends a little

over $1,000,000. I do not know what proportion of the stock is held in Canada; but dividends are paid in this country, so that a very small amount of money is going out of Canada by reason of the fact that a portion of the capital is supplied by citizens of the Unitec' States.
Now the minister proposes, by reducing the duty, to cut down these purchases which art now made in Canada, by making it easier foi the manufacturers to buy from the United States. As shown by a ruling of the Department of Customs, the minister is going to cut the duties on 130 parts by 25 per cent if the manufacturers manufacture fifty per cent of the finished article in Canada. I point this out to the minister: that even though all these manufacturers qualify for that reduction the minister would still be charging the manufacturer who manufactures his car in Canada a higher duty on parts than he will exact from me if I purchased a car in the United States. Let me put it in this way; the minister says to me "'Clark, if you buy a car made in Canada I will see that you pay from 25 per cent to 35 per cent on every part imported from the United States that goes into that car. If that manufacturer happens to make fifty per cent of your car in Canada I will give him a rebate of 25 per cent, but if you will buy a car that is fully manufactured in the United States, made by American workmen, with American capital, I will charge you only 20 per cent duty." Has there ever been an instance where this government has subsidized American manufacturers in preference to Canadian manufacturers? This is a case where the minister is subsidizing American manufacturers, encouraging Canadians to buy American cars, because if they do so they will pay less duty on parts than they will pay if they purchase Canadian cars. These are some of the reasons why the minister's suggestion of a rebate is of no value. I may point out that only four out of 134 articles will come into Canada at a 20 per cent duty, namely, the automobile cover, the body, the chassis and the wheels. There are 130 other parts which -will come in at the old duty.
Before I was interrupted by the Minister of Finance I was giving some reasons why cars manufactured in Canada cost more than cars manufactured in the United States. Another reason is the high taxation in Canada. It lias been generally admitted that about twenty-five cents out of every dollar of our net production goes into taxes, municipal, provincial or federal. There is an enormous tax on industry, and I showed quite clearly before the House

The Budget-Mr. Clark
took recess that that taxation, largely falls upon corporations and manufacturers and the result is to increase materially the cost of . manufacture in Canada.
Another reason is the cost of distribution. The minister knows that we have a wide area over which to distribute motor cars. Then we have the fact that the freight rates from Toronto to Vancouver are enormously high, compared to those paid in the state of New York by manufacturers there, or by the manufacturers in Detroit in the state of Michigan. Our large area and sparse population also accounts for the increased cost of selling a car in Canada as compared with the United States. I venture to say that on a car which costs $2,000 in Canada, at least $100 of the additional cost to the consumer is the extra cost due to the increased commission paid to dealers. Add to that the extra freight charges and you have an enormously increased percentage cost to the Canadian consumer of a Canadian car. Furthermore much of the misunderstanding which has arisen in connection with motor cars and their cost is due to the fact that the Canadian consumer must pay the five per cent sales tax, the five per cent luxury tax on cars under $1,200, the ten per cent luxury tax on cars over $1,200, making ten per cent on cars under $1,200 and fifteen per cent on cars over $1,200. We are inclined to compare the cost to us of a car delivered in the outlying parts of Canada with the price at which an American may buy his car in the state in which it is manufactured without any of the taxes, except the three per cent luxury tax. Nothing could be more unfair than that.
Another reason why the-cost of manufacture in Canada is greater than in the United States is the mass production. For instance, twenty-five cars are produced by Ford in Detroit to every one produced in Ford, Ontario. If any of my hon. friends were manufacturing, for instance, binders, and had a factory which could produce only one binder a day, and I have a factory where I can produce twenty-five binders a day, in which factory do they think we would get the more efficiency and the cheaper binder? I venture to say it would be in my factory. With efficient management, if I were manufacturing twenty-five binders a day, and one of my Saskatchewan friends was producing one a day in his factory, I venture to say I could produce my binder anywhere from twenty per cent to twenty-five per cent cheaper than he could manufacture his.
Now Mr. Speaker, what protection is left to the automobile industry in Canada? I should like to take one practical illustration
of a car which is manufactured in Canada. Take, for example, the Overland five-passenger touring car. Under the tariff as it now stands at 35 per cent, the duty on that car is $136; under the revised tariff it will pay $77.70. It so happens that the Overland Company import parts for the manufacture of that particular car on which they pay duties to the amount of $74. I hope my hon. friend will follow me.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am following the hon. member. I would like to know on what valuation he bases that $136?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: On the valuation on which the tariff is charged, which I think is the price to the wholesaler from the factory. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I want to know in dollars and cents what is the value of the car.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend the exact value-somewhere around $400 or $420. But I do know-if my hon. friend will investigate he will ascertain the fact-that the duty now paid on an Overland five-passenger touring car is $136; that the duty on the same car when this tariff goes into effect, if it does go into effect, will be $77.70, and that the duty paid on parts which go into the manufacture of that car is $74. That leaves for the company a protection of exactly $3.70; in other words their protection is wiped out at one fell swoop by the drastic reduction of 42 per cent. I ask my hon. friend what is going to be the effect of this reduction upon the British investor-perhaps not the British investor because it does not come home to him so much, but the American investor-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Before my hon. friend proceeds with the argument, in the $74 duty on the parts has he allowed the 25 per cent drawback?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
No I have not, because in
this particular car I believe fifty per cent is not manufactured in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Then I admit frankly that
we intend that these companies shall manufacture fifty per cent in Canada. That is the idea.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That is an arbitrary statement on the part of the minister irrespective of whether or not it is possible for companies to do that. I thought I had elaborated that portion of my argument, that some companies started out simply as assembling plants in which not more than ten per cent of the total value would be manufactured in Canada. That percentage is gradually being increased. In fact an increase is necessary in order to take
The Budget-Mr. Clark

advantage of the British preference which requires 25 per cent Canadian workmanship and material and which I understand will be increased in the near future. I also know and my hon. friend knows it is the ambition of every manufacturer to increase his percentage of production in Canada. For example, a company which three or four years ago had just installed itself in Canada and was doing say only ten per cent of the production here, and has to-day worked1 up to thirty per cent, a laudable increase-that company to-day, if it is in the position of the company to which I have just referred, has its protection absolutely wiped out. by this budget. It is not even given an opportunity of increasing its production to fifty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: How can my hon. friend argue in favour of industries getting away with manufacturing only ten or twenty-five per cent in Canada and in the next breath condemn the British preference because we allow goods to come in with only twenty-five per cent being manufactured in England?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I have not condemned the
British preference. When did I condemn it?
Mr. ROiBB:	A party over there has.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I will not get into an argument with the minister over the British preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: He had better not.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That is a big subject. I
do not fear for one moment debating that subject with the minister, but he is in a position now where he knows he has done an injustice to a certain industry and he-is not willing to stick to that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I propose to confine myself to it. As regards the British preference on this particular thing, I am willing to engage my hon. friend on it. I have shown distinctly, I think, that the Minister of Finance and his government have wiped out the protection for the average car manufactured in Canada. I have shown that by a concrete illustration which he cannot refute and which no member of his ministry can refute.
I am sorry the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) is not in the House to-day, because I was particularly interested in a remark which he let fall the other day when the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) was speaking on this matter. The hon. member for Fort William stated that this export trade with Great Britain was of great advantage to Canada. The hon. member for 
Brandon interrupted saying:	That weakens
your argument. I presume what he meant was this, that because we can export to England in competition with United States manufacturers, we should therefore be able to compete with them in Canada without protection, or with the protection we have, or with the protection which is proposed. I know quite well the hon. member for Brandon has not made a study of the question or he never would have made that observation.
In the British market under the British preference we have to-day an advantage over our United States competitors of 11% per cent. I showed this afternoon by a reference to the drawback of customs given for parts imported from the United States on a Canadian car going into the British market, the cost of manufacture of a car in Canada for distribution to the Canadian people is increased by sixteen per cent. In other words, a Canadian manufacturer who gets a drawback on his parts for cars for export, gets sixteen per cent of the total cost of production of these cars for export refunded to him by the Customs department. That gives him another sixteen per cent protection in the British market as against the United States manufacturer, a protection of sixteen per cent that he does not get in the Canadian market on cars which he manufactures for Canadian trade. That makes in all a protection of 27% per cent on those two features alone, which the Canadian manufacturer gets in the British market over his United States competitor. That is why the Canadian manufacturer is able to export cars to Great Britain and compete in that market with the United States manufacturer, and that is also why the Canadian manufacturer can sell his cars cheaper in the British market under the British preference than he can afford to sell them in the Canadian market.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Hoes the hon.

I do not intend to make,
my speech over again; I was cross-examined on that point this afternoon. In the light * of the industry's experience since other reductions have been made we should not sacrifice any other industry of great importance without due investigation. When I recall the effect of reductions on other industries, such as the woollen and steel industries as well as industries in my own constituency, I am convinced that the government is taking a fatal step in making the present proposed reduction without investigation. I believe it was in 1923 that this government cut the tariff on saw-mill machinery. My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) made the statement in this House that because of that reduction many new mills had been built in British Columbia; I absolutely dispute that suggestion. Indeed, as a result of the reduction, several industries in Vancouver have been closed down. One firm which manufactured logging engines, with an output of two engines per month, was supplying the trade in British Columbia, and it was obliged to close down within six months of the tariff cut. That industry to-day employs only four men who are engaged in repairing logging engines imported from the United States, and the proprietor is acting as agent for an American manufacturer of the very article which he himself formerly turned out.
Take the steel industry also. This is undoubtedly a basic industry, if any is, and we

The Budget-Mr. Clark
find that far from there having been any progress there has been a retrograde movement in this case since the present government came into office. In the calendar year of 1912 Canada produced 821,000 gross tons of steel ingots; in 1913 this had increased to 1,066,000 tons. In 1923 the production in this industry had fallen off to 840,000 tons and in 1924 there was a further shrinkage to 625,000 tons.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The result of the reduction
was that imports from the United States increased. And what has been going on in the steel industry in the United States at the same time? In fifteen years we find that while Canada has been standing still in the steel industiy, the increase in United States production has been 75 per cent. It might be well at this point for me to refer to the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) yesterday in claiming credit for the great advances in the stock market last year. Well, recently there has been a dreadful slump, and I am not sure that it is not equal to the' advance of last year; it certainly is in those industries affected by this government's tariff policy. I am advised by authorities who should know that there is now in progress very heavy selling of Canadian securities, due to the new provision respecting income tax on Canadian investments. This action of the government will drive a large amount of capital out of Canada for investment in American securities, and the people who so invest will probably open American bank accounts and leave their money in the United States, thus escaping Canadian income tax on their American investments. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance in suggesting that he has done this to enable our capitalists to reinvest their money in Canadian securities must know that his suggestion is a joke; it cannot be done.
What is the situation in Canada to-day?' We find our crops have been good. Does the government suggest that it was responsible for the increased production of the soil last year? ^ We find the pulp and paper industry is thriving. Well, that industry will thrive until the natural resources on which it depends are exhausted. If my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior will examine the records in his own department, he will find his experts estimate that within our own time the available accessible supply of pulpwood

The Budget

Mr. Totzke
in this country will be exhausted. We have a greater production also in the mining industry and in the fishing industry. Those are about the only industries in Canada that are making progress. But let me point out that they are all wasting industries. Take, for instance, the mining industry, we have Cobalt worked out and the industry receding into the Porcupine, and now into the Red Lake district. We have other examples in the Yukon and the Rossland mining camps. We have another example in the fishing industry on the Fraser river. A few years ago you could see from the train millions of fish in that river; to-day, Mr. Speaker, as you know from your own investigations that is no longer the case.
To-day my friends from Saskatchewan are jubilant because of their great wheat crop last year and because of their control of the world's market in that commodity; but I warn them that when Russia is reorganized she will be again a formidable competitor in the wheat market of the world, and that market is not likely to expand.
Bearing all these things in mind, Mr. Speaker, we should devote ourselves to a more diversified industrial development. With the example of exhausted natural resources in other countries, one would think Canadians would make it their first concern to manufacture their natural resources at home and make it possible for the country to support a larger population and produce greater wealth. Since this government came into office it has driven over 500,000 young Canadians, the very best of our stock, to the United States because it has preferred to encourage American industry at the expense of Canadian.
My friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) yesterday referred in jubilant tones to the fact that the income tax has been practically wiped out on incomes equal to a member of parliament's indemnity, and he added in great glee, " Keep your eye on the price of motor cars." My plea, Sir, is that the members of this House and the people of the Dominion keep their eye on the employees in those factories who are now being affected by the tariff reductions on motor cars; that they keep their eye on the unemployment that will result; that they keep their eye on the distress that will follow; and that they keep their eye on the exodus to the United States due to the closing of five industries in the city of Oshawa alone. My further plea is that they join with the Conservative party in a determined effort to enforce the fulfilment of the solemn pledge given by this government that no industry shall suffer a reduction of its tariff protection until a proper investigation has been made by
the recently appointed Tarm .revisory Board. How long, Mr. Speaker, are protectionist constituencies such as North Waterloo, Joliette and North Vancouver going to send representatives to this House who, while they profess to be protectionists, help to install in office a Prime Minister who has no respect for his pledge, a Prime Minister who solemnly promises that Canadian industries shall get a fair deal and full opportunity to be heard before their tariff protection is taken away or diminished,-I say how long are those and other protectionist constituencies going to send members to this House to support such a Prime Minister,-members who protest when tariff reductions are made, but nevertheless render the reductions possible by remaining with a party which breaks its pledges?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to occupy very much time in this my first address, but there are a few things in connection with the budget that I feel I should discuss very briefly.	Let me first of all
congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon his very excellent budget.
I think I can safely say that this budget is very pleasing to at least ninety per cent of the people of Canada. Not only is the budget itself very welcome but the improved financial conditions which made this budget possible are very gratifying. More especially is that so, Mr. Speaker, after the blue ruin speeches which we heard throughout the length and breadth of the country during the recent election campaign, and even during this present session. We were told that the factories were being closed, that trade was falling off, and that the country generally was on the verge of ruin. So it is very gratifying that the Finance minister is able to bring down a budget making a reduction of some $25,000,000 in taxation. We know that revenues are required to carry on the business of this country, and it is gratifying indeed to note that business has already so improved, and that the prospects for business in the future are so bright, that the Minister of Finance has been able to make the reductions now' proposed in the budget. Not only are the majority of the people pleased with the budget, but I am sure that if our friends opposite would only give candid expression to their opinions they would also admit satisfaction.
One of the items of the budget which to my mind is of importance to the constituency which I represent is the reduction in the income tax levied on the man with a small income. The chief occupation of the people
The Budget-Mr. Totzke

in my constituency, as is the case with the majority of the people in the province from which I come, is that of farming. The farmer of the western prairies, with the conditions obtaining and the class of farming carried .on, is in the position that one year he will have good crops and splendid returns and will have to pay a large income tax, then possibly for the next two or three years he has to operate his farm at a small profit or in some cases at a loss. So he may pay income tax one year and operate at a loss the following year, and there is no allowance made for this difference. I do not know that this could be remedied in any way, but I do know that the increase in exemptions will do much to alleviate this condition.
Some hon. members of the opposition have stated that the reductions in the income tax are only apparent; that while the reductions apply to the man with the small income the tax is increased when applied to 9 p.m. incomes derived from dividends or other unearned sources. I submit that this is as it should be. It is the man with the small income, who is raising a family and trying to give his children a proper education which will fit them to become good and useful citizens-and these comprise by far the greater part of our population-who should be given every encouragement possible.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) speaking on the budget the other day, said that this government could not be given the credit for the improved conditions existing in Canada, but that the credit should be given to a munificent Providence. I am ready to admit that Providence had a lot to do with the improved condition of affairs, but had conditions been worse the blame would certainly have been laid on this government, so why should they not receive some credit? There is a saying that the Lord helps those who help themselves, and I submit that the improved condition in which we find ourselves is due in large measure to the economical and careful administration of the government.
I would like to say just a few words in regard to the tariff proposals. This is a very important matter to us in western Canada, as indeed it is to all parte of our Dominion. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has on several occasions paid considerable attention to those sitting in this corner of the House; he has called us the Saskatchewan colony, and free traders. I do not know just what he means by "Saskatchewan colony"; I do not think he intends to be very complimentary, but I want to say 
that this Saskatchewan colony will keep on growing. Most important of all, there is absolute harmony amongst ourselves; we are all here with one purpose. That purpose is not to impose our will upon this government or upon tlie rest of Canada, but to secure fair treatment as we are wdlling to accord fair treatment to others. The right hon. gentleman has called us free traders. Perhaps our inclinations are for free trade, because we cannot see that protection can be of any benefit to us. Our main business is the production of wheat; we are gradually getting into mixed farming, and that class of farm work has already assumed considerable proportions, but the main thing is still the production of wheat. When we sell our wheat we must sell it on the open market, in competition with the rest of the world, so we cannot see any advantage to be gained by having protection. In that way perhaps the hon. gentleman is partially correct when he diasses us as free traders. Our inclinations are for free trade, just as the inclinations of those in the industrial centres are for protection, because they believe protection is to their advantage. Let me say, however, that while our inclinations may be for free trade, we have not come here expecting to get free trade, nor do we expect to get any drastic cut in the tariff at present.
The voters in Saskatchewan demonstrated one thing last October, that is, that they do not desire any increase in these tariff duties. The leader of the Conservative party preached higher tariffs, and so far as the people of Saskatchewan are concerned he has his answer; not a Conservative member from that province is in this House. A great deal has been said' during this session with regard to the popular vote cast last October; members of the opposition have gleefully counted the votes cast in opposition to the government candidates, and in so doing have counted the votes cast for Progressives. In my constituency we had a three-cornered fight, with Liberal, Progressive and Conservative candidates. The Conservative lost his deposit, and I venture to say that had the Progressive candidate not run, the Conservative would not have gained fifty votes. It seems to me the votes cast in Saskatchewan last October were not so much in favour of free trade as in favour of a reasonable tariff, and strongly in opposition to any increase in the tariff duties. We have no desire to injure the business of the manufacturers of this country. We want to see them prosper, and we hope some day to have them in our part of the Dominion. But we do abject to having them make unreasonable profit at our expense.

The Budget-Mr. Totzke
Most, of the time this afternoon was taken up with a discussion of the tariff reduction on automobiles. I do not intend to weary the House by going into a detailed consideration of the matter, but I wish to place on Hansard a statement attributed to Mr. Henry Ford which appeared in the press of to-day. It is a Canadian Press despatch dated Detroit, April 21st, and reads as follows:
Henry Ford, Detroit industrial magnate, this afternoon stated his belief that the industry at Ford city would "run better if there were no tariff whatever." Mr. Ford declared himself to be a free trader. The magnate was interviewed on the Walkerviille ferry as he was returning from an inspection trip of the Ford city plant. He would add nothing to the statement made by Mr. Wallace R. Campbell, general manager and treasurer of the Ford Motor Company of Canada, other than expressing the opinion that free trade would be best tor the Canadian plant.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman
aware that Mr. Ford owns only about twenty per cent of the Canadian stock, and the whole of the American stock; that they are two separate companies, and that he might be quite willing to have the Canadian plant closed?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I do not wish to discuss the matter with the hon. gentleman at all except to say that the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon are answered, I think, by the statement in the despatch quoted that " free trade would be best for the Canadian plant The Saskatchewan members came down here to discuss matters with our eastern friends. We came animated by the spirit of give and take, and the sooner our eastern friends get away from the idea that we are looking for free trade the better it will be for all of us. We understand the conditions in eastern Canada perhaps better than easterners understand conditions in the west, for the reason that a good many of us were born and raised in the eastern part of the Dominion. I myself was bom and brought up in Kitchener, which is one of the best industrial centres in this old province of Ontario. One of the members of the opposition made the suggestion some weeks ago that it might be a good thing for the members of this House to travel to various parts of Canada and become acquainted with the conditions in each locality. I believe that idea could be acted upon to advantage, and that it would result in a better understanding between the east and the west.
The improvement in the finances of the Canadian National Railways, as announced by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech is also very gratifying. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) when
speaking the other day, expressed satisfaction with the improved conditions of the railway, but he did what our friends opposite usually do whenever this government does anything worth while: He tried to prove that in some way the credit is due to the party on that side of the House. The hon. gentleman said on the occasion referred to that while this road was in good shape and its condition was improving day by day, the credit for that really should be given to the right hon. leader of the opposition. Well, Mr. Speaker, we are not so much concerned as to who gets the credit for the improved condition of the railway as we are with the condition itself. While perhaps the right hon. leader of the opposition was the father of the road, the present conditions prove that sometimes a foster father is better able to care for a child than a natural father. From the way things were going on when this government came into power I am afraid that had the child been left with its father much longer it would have been in a pretty ragged and dilapidated condition, or perhaps would have been swallowed up altogether by the wolves.
To my mind the government made a happy selection when they secured the services of Sir Henry Thornton as general manager. He has been able to imbue the officials of the road with a different spirit, and those of us who patronize this road can testify to the courtesy and efficient service now given. Let me tell hon. members a little experience I had on my trip west during the last recess. I was going from Winnipeg to Saskatoon. Getting up in the morning I met the porter in the corridor and I said "Are we running on time this morning, porter?" His answer was "Yes, indeed, sir-the 'National way'." That is an illustration of the spirit that exists on this national railway to-day, and if it is all that Sir Henry Thornton has been able to do it has been well worth while; it makes all the difference between operating the line on a paying basis and on a non-paying basis.
The hon. member for South York (Mr. MaClean, who is perhaps the most consistent advocate of public ownership in this House, makes a plea for the amalgamation of the two roads, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. He claims that some $250,000,000 could be saved annually by removing duplication of the service. I am ready to support the hon. gentleman on the question of public ownership, but I cannot support the amalgamation of these two roads. I think the hon. gentleman would find that when he came to do away with the duplication of the two systems there would be such a howl of

The Budget-Mr. Totzke
protest, such a storm of opposition, that to carry that suggestion into effect would be almost impossible. Perhaps in very few cases it could be done, but here is the situation you have to meet. In very many instances there are towns built along these lines. There are shipping facilities, elevators, and all that goes to make up the small towns of the western prairies. While these places are small they are very important and do a lot of business. So that I cannot agree with my hon. friend's scheme of doing away with the duplication of service. I will admit that there are instances where the passenger service on the lines, or something of that character, might be diminished, but the lines themselves could not be done away with.
Furthermore, there is the question of competition. Competition is the life of trade, and to us in the west of Canada competition means a lot, especially during the harvest time when our rush season is on and we require a great number of cars. Let me give an illustration of how the lack of competition sometimes works out to the detriment of the settlers. In one corner of my constituency there is a railroad grade that was built in 1912 and 1913. The grade is there for some twenty-five or thirty miles, but there is no steel on it and I will tell you why. The particular district this railway was supposed to serve has been settled ever since 1898 when the first batch of settlers went in there. They are good settlers, they have improved their farms, and they have done well. When they went in the Canadian Northern, as it was then, built the main line, known as the Winnipeg and Edmonton railway, just to the south of this district. The Canadian. Northern also secured a lease of the Regina and Prince Albert branch, which was the old Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific had the line from Young to Prince Albert. While this condition existed, the Canadian Northern with lines on two sides of the triangle, and the Grand Trunk Pacific on the other-or rather I should say this rectangle, because the Canadian Northern had another line on the north side of it-there was competition between these two roads. And the Canadian Northern constructed this grade with the purpose of securing the grain from that particular district. Since the amalgamation this particular section of the country is surrounded on four sides by one road, the Canadian National. There is no longer any need, so far as the railway is concerned, to construct that road, but the settlers need it. They have from twenty-five to thirty miles [Mr Totzke.]
to haul their grain, and anyone living in the west knows it is not profitable to haul grain for more than ten or twelve miles. So that since the Canadian National have had these four lines this grade has been lying there idle, and I submit that if one of these lines had remained in competition with the Canadian National the condition would be much better. This particular branch line was included three sessions ago in the branch lines railway bill, but the proposal for its construction was thrown out by the Senate. I am in hopes that before long, with improved conditions in the country generally, and in our National railway operation in particular, it will not be long before they undertake the construction of that line.	[DOT]
Just a few words on the subject which was really the main issue in the campaign last October in my constituency, namely the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. I am not going fully into the matter of the completion of this road or the matter of its feasibility or cost, but I wish to make one or two references to the matter. As I said before, in our election campaign three candidates were seeking election, and the main plank in the platform of each one of them was the completion of the Hudson Bay road. I observe the right hon. leader of the opposition is not in his seat I wanted to draw this particularly to his attention. I desire to read a statement from the platform of the Conservative candidate in that constituency. It will be taken for granted that the Progressive and the Liberal candidates would certainly be in favour of the immediate completion of that road, because that has been a plank in our platform ; it has been our desire for years to have the line completed. The following advertisement appeared in the Bruno Leader of October 8, 1925:
Mr. E. S. Wilson, the Conservative candidate for the federal constituency of Humboldt, stands for:
1. Immediate completion of the Hudson Bay railway.
But that is not the best of this particular article; there is a paragraph at the bottom of the article which reads:
These are the policies laid down by the leader of the Conservative party and endorsed by the Conservative candidate for Humboldt.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am just introducing that to show my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition the feeling of the people in my constituency. I might say further that that is the feeling of the vast majority of the people of Saskatchewan, the province from which I come. If by any chance the candidate of the leader of the opposition in the constituency of Humboldt had been elected,

The Budget-Mr. McGibbon
he would have had at least one man sitting behind him who was pledged to support the immediate completion of the Hudson Bay railway. Indeed I believe he has several right now wrho are pledged to the completion of this road.
There is considerable opposition, Mr. Speaker, in eastern Canada to the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. A lot of propaganda has been printed, and it might be interesting to know just where the money comes from to pay for that propaganda. It is feared by those in the eastern provinces that the completion of this road will perhaps mean the diversion of traffic from eastern ports and subsequent depreciation in value of the terminals and shipping facilities in those provinces. To my mind there is no occasion for eastern interests to be alarmed on that score. Even after the road is completed, we realize that we will not be able to ship our grain and cattle immediately. It will take some time to get the proper facilities, and by the time there is any big movement of grain out of that port our production will have increased to such an extent that it cannot all go through the Hudson Bay route, and we will need every avenue through which we can possibly export our produce. We are not only advocating the completion of this road for the transportation of our grain and cattle; we believe the natural resources in forests, minerals, fish and agriculture that will be developed will justify its completion. Let me read a clipping which will illustrate to some extent what I mean. I do not know whether to take this article at its face value, but I wish to read it to the House to show that it is not only the farmers in western Canada who think this road would be a beneficial proposition, but that others are of the same opinion. I have here a Canadian Press report dated January 27, which reads in . this way:
Toronto, Jan. 27.-"If I were out of work to-day, I would go straight to the Hudson's Bay district," said Professor A. Fitzpatrick of the Frontier College at the social service council convention here, to-day.
"There is work and to spare for millions if they have the right clothing which would cost $100 a man."
Professor Fitzpatrick predicted there would be half a dozen cities on the Hudson bay in the next decade or two, each one a quarter of the size of Toronto.
"You will live to see half a dozen railways to Hudson bay. So soon as the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway is pushed on to Moose Factory the Canadian Pacific Railway and others will be forced to build connection too," he said.
"The Hudson bay itself will easily support one million people." .
He proposed that the social service council should do something practical next year by putting 1,000 jobless men with sufficient clothing arid equipment for the work which is always waiting for them in cutting pulp-wood in the new northern country.
As I said before, we believe that this line when completed to the Hudson bay alone will support itself, whether or not it is a feasible road for our grain and cattle. We believe it is feasible, and we have abundant information in connection with that, but I do not intend to take up time discussing it. Perhaps we will have an opportunity later on to do so.
The right hon. leader of the opposition has told the Saskatchewan members in this corner of the House that we would find before we were here very long that we could not get what we want from the government. May 1 say in conclusion that we have got and are getting what we want from the government and our good friends from the eastern and other parts of this country. That is the consideration of our problems and the opportunity of discussing with them the problems of other parts of the Dominion with a view to assisting in finding some solution for them. We realize that we are not the only province in this Dominion, and it is only by co-operation and mutual concession and goodwill that our country will gain the great position amongst the nations of the world to which it is entitled.

I have heard the hon. member ask that question three or four times to-day. I was hoping he had something else in his repertoire. Why, sure, I would put the duty back until the Tariff Advisory Board appointed by the government had an opportunity to look fully into the question. 1 believe in giving every Canadian industry protection enough to carry on. We are giving protection to the western farmers in the way of freight rates, and I submit that the industries of Ontario have an equal right to live. This question, Sir, as the late leader of the Progressive party in this House once said, is elementary in its simplicity. Now, I ask the minister: Does he think with all his knowledge and experience that he is able, without any evidence, to render a verdict upon any issue of that kind Is it fair to himself, is it fair to the country, i3 it fair to any industry for him to just get up and say, "The people believe you are enjoying too much protection, and we are going to take the duty off, although we do not know whether you have got too much protection; we do not even know if you have got enough"? Why Mr. Speaker, such an attitude is ridiculous. The thing is ridiculous. To my mind it would have been much nearer the truth had he said that the Minister of Railways demanded it, and the government had to give it to him. We know that he, the Minister of Railways, and the members from Saskatchewan have come down here demanding not the head of Barabbas but the head of industrial Ontario, and there is more than a suspicion that thjis budget js. an election budget, reflecting the feeling of this government towards the province of Ontario because of what happened on October 29 last. I ask the minister what reason he can give? Surely he can give some reason for jeopardizing the 14011-173
employment of 22,000 men and the living of 100,000 people without even a trial. Is not the thing absurd?
I do not wish to follow that line further, as it is getting late. I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture is not in his place, because I had intended to give him some information whereby he could stir the dry bones of that department and make it of some use to the Canadian people. This government, by its action and inaction, has practically wiped out the protection of our farmers, and they have been left exposed to the cheap Australian and New Zealand butter which is ruining the market. Had the minister been here I would have read a clipping from the Toronto Globe under yesterday's date, in which it is stated that the western provinces of British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta are flooded with Australian butter; that the western Canadian butter is drifting down into Toronto, and that the price is down to 33 and 34 cents a pound. That is the result of legislation passed by this government.
Before going into that I would like to refer again to the Minister of Finance. He has stated that he does not know how to find out what protection these industries require, so I am going to tell him where to get some examples. I have in my hand the regulations under the Safeguarding of Industries Act of Great Britain, which I will read in order to give the minister some idea of how to proceed. When an industry applies for protection the evidence is to be heard and the verdict rendered on the following conditions:
(1)	Whether the applicant industry is, by reason of the volume of employment engaged in the production of the goods to which the application relates, or by reason of the nature of the goods produced, an industry of substantial importance.
(2)	Whether foreign goods of the class or description to which the application relates are being imported into and retained for consumption in the United Kingdom in abnormal quantities.
(3)	Whether the foreign goods so imported are being sold or offered for sale in the United Kingdom at prices which are below the prices at which similar goods can be profitably manufactured or produced in the United Kingdom.
(4)	Whether, by reason of the severity and extent of such competition, employment in the manufacture or production of such goods in the United Kingdom is being, or is likely to be, seriously affected.
(5)	Whether such exceptional competition comes largely from countries where the conditions are so different from those in this country as to render the competition unfair.
Competition for the purpose of such inquiry is not to be deemed to be unfair unless it arises from one or more of the following causes
(a)	Depreciation of currency operating so as to create an export bounty.
(b)	Subsidies, bounties, or other artificial advantages.
(c)	Inferior conditions of employment of labour. . .



The Budget-Mr. McGibbon
I have here the report on the cutlery industry, which applied for protection, and we find the verdict as follows:
In all the circumstances, we consider that a duty of 33% per cent ad valorem would be reasonably sufficient -and we recommend that such a duty should be imposed for a period of at least five years.
That is the way they find out in Great Britain whether or not an industry needs protection, what protection it needs,
10 p.m. and for how long it is needed.
I recommend that system to the Minister of Finance. I have also a report on the aluminium industry, and after hearing the evidence this is what they say:
We are not in a position to state that the applicant industry has established a claim to a duty.
It works both ways, as you see. I have also a report on the wrapping paper industry, and I find that the verdict is as follows:
We recommend a duty of 17J per cent-
In the glove industry I find a double verdict rendered. On the question of leather gloves they say:
We therefore recommend that a duty of 33% per oent ad valorem should be imposed for at least five years.
On the question of fabric gloves, in the same verdict they say:
We do not recommend a duty on fabric gloves of silk and artificial silk.
I recommend to the minister that he get his information along these lines, and he will then be in a position to give this House the reasons for the reduction or increase in duty upon any article in a reasonable way, not in the unreasonable way which he followed this afternoon.
I want to deal now with the United States. I have the seventh annual report of the United States tariff commission and I want to read their instructions. Section 315 of the Tariff Act of 1922 provides:
"In order to regulate the foreign commerce of the United States and put into force and effect the policy of the Congress by this act intended," the President shall have power, upon investigation, to ascertain the differences in costs of production of domestic articles and of like or similar imported articles and to proclaim the changes in classification or increases or decreases in rates of duty which may be necessary to equalize the differences in costs thus ascertained.
Those instructions were given to the United States tariff commission, which President Harding called the greatest advance in tariff making in the last hundred years. What is the result? The president has power to either raise or decrease the duties or to alter the classification up to 50 per cent, but he cannot do that-and this is the point I want to impress upon the Minister of Finance-until an investigation has been held. That is the way these things are settled in Great Britain and the United States, and I recommend that procedure to the government of this country. If that course is adopted they can come to parliament and give reasons for their actions, and they will not slaughter an industry, as has been done in the case of the automobile industry, simply because they say the public believes it should be slaughtered. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that such reasons are beneatu any man holding the position of finance minister of any country on God's earth.
For a few moments, Mr. Speaker, I want to take up something on behalf of the farmers of this country. I did want to show the Minister of Agriculture how he could do something for our farmers. I have carefully gone through the workings of the Fordney-McCumber tariff as it applies to the farmers of the United States, and when I am told in this House that farmers cannot be protected by tariff I want hon. members to read these figures, which I am going to ask leave to place on Hansard. Now that tariff came into force, as most hon. gentlemen know, on May 27, 1921. To be brief let me say this: I have gone through every branch of the farming industry in the United States from wheat to cotton, and with two exceptions-those were milk and cheese, where the duty had not been raised sufficiently-in every case the tariff raised the price of the farm products of the United States, and in many cases raised it by the amount of the duty.

speechtext:
The same influence as any other food has. Now then what happened? Imports before 1913 were less than 100,000 bushels a year. They made them free in that year, and the imports thereupon rose to 12,290,000, and from 1915 to 1920 they averaged 5,210,000 bushels. After the tariff went on, what happened? Only 91,000 bushels

came in. And what was the the effect on the price? Before that, down in Buenos Aires, the other market for it, the price was 25 cents more than the price in Chicago, and after that the United States price went ahead of the price in Buenos Aires. That was the effect on corn-a difference of twenty-five cents a bushel.
Now I take up the question of cheese. The duty on cheese was not raised to any considerable extent. It was increased from 20 per cent to 23 per cent, but the change was not sufficient to have any effect on the price. We see practically the same result in regard to milk, because the duty was only two cents a gallon and it had no effect on the price. Now we come to beans. The duty on beans was raised from 25 cents a bushel to $1.20. In 1920, before the duty went on, the imports were 2,094,646 bushels. In 1921, after the duty was imposed, the imports dropped to 274,058 bushels, and the price rose from four to seven cents a pound. That is what the tariff did for the farmers in the United States in regard to beans. Then I come to wool, and I find that the raise in the tariff made an increase in price of 25 to 35 cents a pound. One of the greatest industries of the United States is cotton. The effect that the tariff had on cotton was to raise the price six or seven cents a pound. That is what it put into the pockets of the man who was growing cotton.
I have a good deal more information as to other articles, but I have given enough. The point is that the American republic, by reason of the fact that they have a scientific board which is working day and night studying these questions and applying scientifically the principles of their tariff policy, have increased the price of practically every farm product in that country and have put hundreds of millions of dollars in the pockets of their farmers. I wish the Minister of Agriculture were present to-night; I would like to get into his head the idea that the farmers of the country can be protected as much and more than any other class of people, and it is on their behalf I am speaking now. I have not used half the material I have here before me, but I think I have used enough to show this government that what it wants is a scientific tariff board to tell us when duties should go up and when they should come down, and that tariff board should apply not only to industry but also to the great farming population of this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Everybody accepts that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It is exactly the opposite.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I must insist that the
hon. member quote me properly. This is the third time the hon. member has failed to do so. I said that under conditions of free trade everybody accepts the fact that it is higher m Winnipeg than in the United States.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend said normally under free trade the price of wheat would be higher in Winnipeg than in the United States; therefore I must flatly contradict his statement, for the reason that the United States have a hundred million odd people to feed and in Canada we have only ten million. We have to sell our wheat on an export basis, we * cannot get above it, while in the United States hard wheat is nearly always- in fact you may say always-above an export basis, at a premium. He has made the statement in reply to a question that the United States do export wheat. That is quite true, but it is not hard wheat. There is great demand for their hard wheat to mix with the soft wheat, and they pay a pretty high price for it. Hard wheat is always above the price in Winnipeg; what the Americans are exporting is soft wheat. My hon. friend has given figures in regard to the United States that are absolutely useless, for this reason: they do not take into account the premiums paid for protein. Nearly all the wheat in the United States is handled on a protein basis. The figures referred to what is called a standard price, and that is the
standard price which is paid for wheat with about eleven per cent protein. Then they pay a premium of a few cents up to fifty cents a bushel. That is not taken into account; therefore the figures are entirely useless. If his figures are equally reliable in regard to corn, cheese and other commodities-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
member a question?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Has there been any
change in the relation of protein content to the value of wheat before and after the going into effect of the Fordney-McCumber tariff?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I do not think there has
been very much.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Then what was it that
increased the price?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I will come to that. The
hon. gentleman spent a good deal of time trying to convince the House that when you place a duty on a commodity it usually raises the price. That is what we have been trying to convince our friends for a good many years; yet the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) stated last session or the session before that if we increased the duty on farm implements the price would not be affected, but would remain the same. I am pleased to find that the last speaker agrees with our view of what is sound economics, that under ordinary conditions when you protect an industry or commodity you are going to raise the price. He will not need to spend one minute to convince me that when the United States imposed a duty on Canadian wheat when Canadian wheat was lower in price than the American wheat, the effect was to increase the price to the American farmer. Certainly it was.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The same would apply to
butter.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes. Let me point out, though, that the1 ultimate effect to the United States farmers was quite different from what they expected. They gained something in price on the commodities protected; but the ultimate effect, when they took into consideration the extra price they had to pay for what they purchased, the protected implement, the protected clothing and other protected commodities that they had to buy, meant a net loss to them of $301,000,000. That is, they took the bait, believing that protection was going to help them, was going to enrich them. I suppose it was made very
The Budget-Mr. Millar

attractive by the manufacturing industries of the United States the same as it has been in Canada, and having taken the bait they expected that they were going to reap a great deal of benefit thereby. But when an accounting was made and they found they had suffered a net loss of $301,000,000, I find now that the farmer bloc in the United States have turned against the high tariff and they are crying out against it. I believe they are appealing to congress to make a change.

speechtext: From what authority does this accounting the hon. member speaks of emanate?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The Farm Bureau of the United States.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is that the American Farm Bureau?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Yes.
