speechtext: Located in Chicago?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I do not know where it is located', probably Washington, but I am not sure.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend's figures are away out, because I have the records in my office.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It is a confederation of farmers. It may be located in Chicago. I cannot say where it is located.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The figures are not in line with the figures published bjr the bureau. They may be from some newspaper.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
They were printed, I
believe, in the Grain Growers' Guide as being the official figures from this federation, and I give them as such.
A remark was made by the last speaker (Mr. MoGibbon) regarding the flooding of the prairie provinces with butter from Australia, and I believe he said it was working eastward' into Ontario. I would like to read an extract from a report of a statement made by a trade commissioner from Australia.
Australia is Canada's second best customer, ranking second only to Great Britain, declared Sir James Elder, K.B.E., Australian trade commissioner to the United States, addressing the Canadian Club here to-day.
This is by a representative from Australia to the United States just a few days ago:
"During 1925," said the speaker, "Australia imported $105,000,000 worth of goods from the Dominion,-
That is the Dominion of Canada.
-or an average of $3.60 per capita. And in that same period Canada only sold an average of $3.90 per capita in Great Britain."
Now let us get the comparison between Canada and Australia.

But this trade balance has been all in favour of your country, Canada only importing $6,500,000 worth of Australian products or an average of fourteen cents per capita.
We heard a few minutes ago a statement as to the country being flooded with Australian butter, and we have heard a great deal of that of late. These are the figures of the trade commissioner of Australia himself, who states that Canada during the year imported fourteen cents' worth per capita, while Australia received of Canadian goods $3.60 per capita.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: How many millions?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I gave the figures a moment ago. Australia imported $105,000,000 worth of goods from Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That is an error. There
is a tremendous disparity between the imports and exports and it is much in our favour, but I think it was $19,000,000, or $20,000,000, and not $105,000,000 worth, that we sold to Australia. There is an error there but the hon. member can take it that for say the last six or seven years the disparity has been at least ten to one in our favour. It does not . alter the point.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
If the hon. member is
correct I am willing to accept 'his statement, but I would like to ask if those figures, that is, the $3.60 and the fourteen cents per capita, are also in error.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The comparison would
be about correct.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That serves my purpose
pretty well. In that case, why should we make such a tirade about this country being flooded with Australian butter? I believe this statement is sound, that if all the butter were available for sale at one point in Canada and competition were playing its part, not one pound of Canadian butter would be exported as long as the price in Canada was above an export basis. Who would be foolish enough to export his butter to Great Britain or anywhere else and receive thirty cents a pound when he could sell it right at his door at thirty-two cents a pound? I do not know of anybody who would do that. As long as the price is one cent above export basis, he would sell it at home and the price must come down to export basis before the export of butter would start. That would be the situation if all the butter were available in one place.
But Canada is a big country. There may be a lower price in some provinces, than in others; the price may be higher in one part

The Budget-Mr. Millar
of Canada and lower in another, or at a time when there is a shortage of production, when there is a possibility of cold storage plants cornering the commodity and raising the price, they may take advantage of the situation and export some butter in order to increase the price at home. At no other time is there an opening for Australian butter, because the market that is open to us for the export of our surplus is open also to Australia on equal terms. It is unreasonable to think that Australia would export butter to Canada when the price here is on an export basis, when the same market that is open to us is open to them.
But the provision that is included in the Australia treaty does affect the cold storage' people, and they are the ones who are making the noise. I may add that they have been given considerable assistance by the politicians. In fact I wish the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) was in his seat.
I was in Woodstock a short time ago and some people there were so unkind as to say that he was active in seeing that a little Australian butter was thrown on the market at Woodstock for sale. I do not know about that, but they were unkind enough to say so

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Was it any
better than the cheese he gets in this House?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It is very easy to make
reckless charges in the absence of a member.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Ditto. We must remember
that the hon. member is not always absent. If he wants to make any reply he has an opportunity.
During the past four years we have heard so much about blue ruin and the dry rot that was eating into Canada, we have heard so much about the disaster that would follow in the wake of this government's policy, that we were led to believe that the country was going to the bow-wows: the people were all going to get out and, in short, national bankruptcy would ensue. Some people began to wonder seriously whether there was really anything in these "whispers of death ". They knew that we had passed through strenuous times and that we had a considerable national debt as a result of the war, and they were naturally concerned about the financial condition of Canada. Well, the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) a few days ago has set these fears at rest. Even the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) -I hope I may refer to him in his absence- said he would take no objection to the statement of the Minister of Finance that the condition of Canada had improved in the past four years. From time to time statements have appeared in the press to the effect that our trade returns during that period were much better than they had been before: our post office returns were increasing, as were also the returns from our customs, even with the rotten conditions which have prevailed in that department during several years past, and which will be admitted now in every corner of the House. Even under those conditions the customs returns increased, as did also the clearing house returns. There was a better feeling throughout Canada, according to these reports, and now we have absolute proof that the conditions have improved. This has placed my friends to my immediate right in rather an awkward position. They do not like to admit that they were false prophets; they do not like to admit that the country did not go to the bow-wows. But I am willing to give them credit for being sufficiently Canadian and sufficiently patriotic to find some joy in the fact that the country has improved. How were they to get out of the difficulty? I must confess that I find a great deal of inconsistency in the reasoning of hon. gentlemen to my right. Every time anything bad has happened to Canada the government which has been in power during the past four years was to blame; the country, we were told, reacted at once to the policy put into effect. But if any good fortune fell to the lot of Canada it was because Providence was smilling upon us and the sun was shining; the government were not entitled to any credit. I cannot understand that. Surely it the policy of the government is effective at cue time, if it is going to react upon the country, it will be effective and will react at another. I thought it rather unfair for hon. gentlemen to indulge in this sort of criticism. I know that the government can well defend themselves and I have no brief for them, but it struck me as rather inconsistent that the government should be blamed for everything that was bad while for anything creditable Providence was praised. Whenever there was prosperity it was because of Providence and the virility of the people. Surely when hon. gentlemen prophesied during the past four years they knew that the people were industrious. I can understand that they might go astray in their prophecies if there were many unknown factors to reckon with, but they should at least have known that the people were industrious. Now they seem to be surprised to find that this is so.

The Budget-Mr. Millar
On page 2625 of Hansard the hon. member for Fort William said:
But there is a Providence, they say, which looks after drunken men, and I presume the same Providence looks afiter governments who are drunken with the desire to hold power in spite of the wishes of the people.
If the hon. member had added, would-be governments, there might be some force in what he said. If desire is any guarantee of immunity from danger a number of gentlemen who sit on front benches to my right might climb to the top of the tower of this building and throw themselves over, without dashing their foot against a stone. They would be perfectly safe if desire had any protective charm.
The same hon. member goes on to ask what the workingman and the small farmer are to get out of the budget. It strikes me that this is a workingman's and a small farmer's budget. True, the small farmer may not have an automobile, but the reduction in the customs duty may place an automobile within his reach. That is where many of the small farmers will gain. Does it not ultimately benefit the small man, who has not an income of $3,000, that the man with this income will be relieved of taxation? Is it not well with the small salaried man if the man who employs him, the man with whom he has to deal, is prosperous? Is not the country going to react favourably to such a budget as this? As a matter of fact, is there not already a wave of confidence passing over Canada as a result of the budget proposals? Will not the budget help the man who has not an income of $3,000 and the small farmer who has not an auto? If there is prosperity with some classes, that prosperity will filter through to the small man and there are none who will not feel the effect in the long run. This, to my mind, is the poor man's budget.
The hon. member for Fort William mentioned two instances in which he said the income tax would have an undesirable effect. He referred in the first place to the widow who was receiving an income from dividends. Well, it may be that occasionally in the readjustment an individual may pay a little more now than formerly, but this will happen in very few cases. The fact, however, is that a great many wealthy men have been escaping income taxation in past years by investing their money in such a way as to draw nontaxable dividends. If that is the case the government did a wise thing to tax dividends. The other illustration the hon. member gave was rather amusing. It was that of an old couple who had reached the ages of seventy-three and seventy-four-I am speaking only

from memory, of course,-and who, as I gathered from his remarks, were scraping along on an income of $4,800 a year. I think he said that these people were in the autumn of their days, and he lamented the fact that in the readjustment they would pay $4 more in income tax than they formerly did. Now, surely if dearth of grounds upon which to object is any proof of a good budget this is an excellent one. Just think of the old couple with an income of $4,800 having to pay $4 more than they paid before 1 Is that such a serious matter? There are thousands of couples of seventy-five years of age and over who have worked long and hard in the heat of the day and who have not a quarter of * that to live upon.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Because of the corporations to which you are so friendly. While my leader was speaking an hon. member said to him, referring to the income tax, "So long as you don't have to pay it." I thought that was a harsh remark. I have under my hand figures to show that the farmers of Canada do pay very little income tax. These figures are for 1921, but I suppose what was true then will be largely true now. These are the totals in round figures: employees, $11,000,000; manufacturers, $8,000,000; merchants, including wholesalers and retailers, $7,000,000; professional men, $2,000,000; farmers, $601,000. Although our farmers paid only this comparatively small amount in 1921 it is a considerable increase over what they paid in 1920. It has been thrown in our faces many times that the farmers are not paying income tax. I could pick out homes where the conditions are very sad, and I am sure were I to describe the poverty, the distress and the long hours of labour I would bring tears to your eyes, but I will refrain. There are thousands of our farmers in the east as well as in the west who are slaving long hours and have much less to live on than is enjoyed by the average citizen in a city like Ottawa. When adverse conditions overtook them after the war, particularly in western Canada, when the prices of the commodities they were selling dropped very low while the prices of the commodities they had to buy were still high, many farmers found themselves in straitened circumstances, and in some cases their children had to wear old bags for protection, their parents being too poor to buy them the necessary clothing. In one case a banker told me he went to see a farmer on business and found his wife, formerly a school teacher, out stooking, and she said, "I

The Budget-Mr. Millar
am helping my husband to stook in order to save money enough to buy coal for the winter." And yet because our farmers do not pay a large proportion of the income tax an hon. member says tauntingly, "As long as you don't have to pay it." The money of those farmers has gone in many cases to pay the exorbitant prices that the combines have been able to exact, and with that exaction they have been able to monopolize a great share of the actual wealth and comfort that should belong to all. And yet a few are not satisfied and would throw out such taunts. The farmers are not paying more income tax simply because they have not got the income on which to pay it, not because they are lazy, not because they are indifferent, not because they are inefficient, not because they are failing to do everything they should do to maintain their homes and raise their families. Many a farmer has been compelled frequently to make great personal sacrifices when his family required medical care. Members of the medical profession in this House know that, especially if they are practising in the country. It may be that members of the farmer's family required dental care, but had to do without it for lack of money. In a word, the farmer and his family have to make sacrifices that the average person in our urban centres seldom gives him credit for. After going through such painful experiences it is not a pleasant thing for them to be told they are shirking their duty.
The member for Fort William-perhaps he will read this in Hansard, so I will give him the benefit of it in his absence-made the statement that this government could have removed much more taxation if they had economized more. Well, I remember some three years ago when the hon. member made an excursion into this region of economy and attacked the expenditure involved in sending certain delegates to the Wembley exhibition. Thereupon the ex-whip of the Liberal party, who was interested in the matter, came back at him with some figures that showed apalling extravagance under a former Conservative regime, and, figuratively speaking, the doctor was carried to the hospital after his opponent got through with him. This government is guilty of extravagance, and I know of no government that has not been. This is partly the fault of the governments themselves and partly the fault of the people. What took place in this city not very long ago? Perhaps some of you may not like to hear it, but you are going to. This government discharged some four thousand civil servants during the last four years because of pressure being
brought to bear that the departments had become very much overstaffed since the war. What was the result? I believe that action of the government was a large factor in their losing the two local seats in the last election.
I have heard it said many times that the civil servants almost as a bloc turned against the government. There is the difficulty. When the people reach the high standard that they will say, "We do not want anything for our constituency unless we have a right to it and it will be for the good of Canada as a whole," then we shall have cleaner government. I do not know that the Conservative party has any better record in regard to economy than the Liberal party; perhaps both parties are about equal. But there is one thing the Conservative party did which I have always given them credit for, in fact I have shouted it sometimes from the house tops. I refer to their cleaning up of the Printing Bureau. Every time any government does something that is really courageous in bringing about economy, every section of the House ought to give them credit for it here and in the country, and not take advantage of it at election time.
The hon. member for Fort William propounded a rather strange theory. He said that in some cases if you raised the duty you raised the price, and then if you lowered the duty you again raised the price. He tried to explain it in this way. He said, "You lower the duty"-I do not know whether he mentioned automobiles, but that will serve the purpose as wTell as any other commodity * you lower the duty on automobiles until you ruin the Canadian manufacturer, and immediately the foreign manufacturer will raise his price; so that while you have lowered the duty and destroyed your own industry you find you have to pay a higher price for the foreign made article. Let us analyse that statement. What is it that prevents the Canadian manufacturer of automobiles or of any other commodity charging a higher price now? Is it not the competition of the American manufacturer? If the latter were to raise his price without the duty changing, would not the Canadian manufacturer follow it up immediately? Does anyone believe he would not? If the American manufacturer were to say, "Never mind the duty; I will not sell my commodity in Canada except at an increased price of 10 per cent," do you suppose the Canadian manufacturer would still sell at the same old price? Of course not; he would raise his price at once. The remarks of the hon. member for Fort William may be true where one
